->INTERNAL SENSE<-

2317. **Verse 1.** *And two angels came to Sodom in the evening; and Lot was sitting in the gate of Sodom: and Lot saw them, and rose up to meet them; and he bowed himself with his face toward the ground.* **"Two angels came to Sodom in the evening"** signifies the visitation that precedes judgment. **"Two angels"** signify the Divine Human and the Holy Proceeding of the Lord, to whom judgment belongs. **"Sodom"** signifies the evil, especially those within the Church. **"Evening"** is the time of visitation. **"Lot sitting in the gate of Sodom"** signifies those who are in the good of charity but in external worship; these are represented here by Lot. They are among the evil, but separated from them, which is signified by "sitting in the gate of Sodom." **"Lot saw them"** signifies their conscience. **"He rose up to meet them"** signifies acknowledgment and an affection for charity. **"He bowed himself with his face toward the ground"** signifies humiliation.

2318. **"Two angels came to Sodom in the evening."** That this signifies the visitation <note>term: "Visitation" refers to a spiritual exploration or evaluation of a person or a church’s state before a final judgment occurs.</note> which precedes judgment can be established from what was said by the "three men" (or Jehovah) in the previous chapter, as well as from what follows in this chapter, and also from the meaning of "evening." In the previous chapter, Jehovah said, "I will go down now and see whether they have done [altogether according to the outcry that has come to me]..." <note>original: "Descendam & videbo, num secundum clamorem, qui venit ad Me, fece-"</note>

# CHAPTER NINETEEN

"...whether the inhabitants of Sodom and Gomorrah <note>original: "Amorae"</note> have made a complete end, and if not, I will know," Verses 20–21. By these words, it was shown in the previous chapter that a **Visitation** <note>A "Visitation" refers to a preliminary spiritual exploration or assessment of a person or society's state before a final judgment occurs.</note> precedes judgment. In this chapter, the act of Visitation itself is described, followed by the Judgment, as is clear from what follows. That "Evening" signifies the time of visitation will be seen below. For the meaning of Visitation, and the fact that it precedes Judgment, see number 2242. 

In the previous chapter, we discussed the perverse state of the human race, and the Lord's sorrow and intercession for those who are in evil but still possess some degree of good and truth. Therefore, what follows now concerns the salvation of those who are in some good and truth (represented in this chapter by **Lot**), alongside the destruction of those who are entirely in evil and falsity (signified here by **Sodom** and **Gomorrah**).

**2319.** That the **two angels** signify the Lord's **Divine Human** <note>The "Divine Human" is the concept that the Lord's human nature became fully divine, allowing Him to reach and save humanity.</note> and the **Holy proceeding** from Him <note>Often understood as the Holy Spirit.</note>, to whom judgment belongs, is evident both from the meaning of "angels" in the Word and from the fact that two angels are mentioned here. It was shown previously (n. 1925) that angels in the Word signify a specific Divine essential within the Lord, though the exact meaning depends on the context. That they here signify the Lord's Divine Human and the Holy proceeding from Him is clear because the "three men" who appeared to Abraham represented the Divine Itself, the Divine Human, and the Holy proceeding (n. 2149, 2156, 2288). From this—and because they are called "Jehovah" in Verse 24—as well as from the general meaning of angels, it is plain that the two angels here represent the Lord's Divine Human and the Holy proceeding.

**2320.** Why there were only two angels here, whereas three men appeared to Abraham, is a secret <note>original: "arcanum," a profound spiritual mystery.</note> that cannot be explained in a few words. It can be understood to some extent by the fact that this chapter deals with **Judgment**—specifically the salvation of the faithful and the damnation of the unfaithful. From the Word, it is clear that judgment is performed by the Lord’s Divine Human and the Holy proceeding. 

Regarding the Divine Human, John says: "The Father judges no one, but has committed all judgment to the Son" (John 5:22) <note>original: "Non Pater judicat quemquam, sed judicium omne dedit Filio"</note>; here "the Son" means the Divine Human (see n. 2159). That judgment also belongs to the Holy proceeding from the Lord's Divine Human is also shown in John: "If I go away, I will send the Advocate <note>original: "Paracletum"</note> to you; and when He has come, He will convict the world of sin, and of righteousness, and of judgment" (John 16:8). And that this Holy power proceeds from the Lord is stated by the same author: "He will not speak on His own authority... but He will take of Mine and declare it to you" (John 16:13, 15). This occurred when the Human was made Divine—that is, when the Lord was glorified—as John says: "The Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified" (John 7:39) <note>original: "Nondum erat Spiritus Sanctus, quia Jesus nondum glorificatus est"</note>.

**2321.** The reason judgment is performed by the Lord’s Divine Human and the Holy proceeding is this: the human race could no longer have been saved unless the Lord had come into the world and united the Divine Essence with the Human Essence. Without the Lord’s Human being made Divine, salvation could no longer reach humanity (n. 1999, 2016, 2034, 2035). The Holy power proceeding from the Lord’s Divine Human is what separates the evil from the good; for the evil so fear and dread the Lord’s Holiness that they cannot approach...

# GENESIS

...that thing, but they flee far from it—each according to the profanity within them—into their own hells.

**2322.** That **Sodom** signifies the wicked, and especially those within the Church, is evident from the meaning of "Sodom" as the evil of **self-love** <note>original: "malum amoris sui"</note> (as discussed in numbers 2220 and 2246). Consequently, it refers to those who live in that specific evil. Those who understand the Word of God only through the literal sense might assume that Sodom refers to the filthiness that goes against the order of nature <note>A reference to the historical interpretation of the "sin of Sodom" as homosexuality.</note>; however, in the **internal sense** <note>The "internal sense" is the deeper, spiritual meaning of the Bible that lies beneath the literal stories.</note>, Sodom signifies the evil of self-love. From this particular evil, all other evils of every kind flow out like a fountain. Everything that springs from self-love is called "adultery" in the Word and is described using that term, which will be demonstrated by the passages from the Word cited at the end of this chapter.

**2323.** That **Evening** signifies the time of **visitation** is clear from the meaning of the word "Evening." In the Word, the various states of the Church are compared both to the seasons of the year and the times of day. They are compared to the seasons: summer, autumn, winter, and spring; and to the times of day: noon, evening, night, and morning. These follow a similar pattern. 

The state of the Church called "Evening" is when there is no longer any charity, and consequently, when faith begins to vanish—this is when the Church ceases to exist. This "Evening" is the one followed by **Night** (see n. 22). However, "Evening" is also the time when charity begins to shine—and thus faith—at the birth of a new Church. This "Evening" is the twilight before the morning (see n. 883). 

Thus, "Evening" signifies both states. It is provided by the Lord that whenever one Church ends, a new one arises at that same time. For without a Church existing somewhere on earth, the human race could not survive, because there would be no connection between humanity and Heaven (as shown in n. 468, 637, 931, 2054). 

This chapter deals with both states of the Church: the birth of the new Church (represented by **Lot**) and the destruction of the old (signified by **Sodom** and **Gomorrah**), as is clear from the content. This is why it is stated here that the two angels came to Sodom in the evening. The text records:
*   What happened in the **Evening** (Verses 1 to 3).
*   What happened in the **Night** (Verses 4 to 14).
*   What happened in the **Morning**, or at the rising of the dawn (Verses 15 to 22).
*   What happened after the sun had risen (Verses 23 to 26).

Because "Evening" signifies these states of the Church, it also signifies the **Visitation** <note>original: "Visitatio"</note> that precedes judgment. When judgment is imminent—meaning the salvation of the faithful and the condemnation of the unfaithful—a Visitation or exploration of their character comes first. This is done to see if any charity and faith remain. This Visitation takes place in the "Evening," which is why the Visitation itself is called "Evening," as seen in the book of Zephaniah:

> "Woe to the inhabitants of the seacoast, the nation of the Cherethites! The word of Jehovah is against you, O Canaan, land of the Philistines; I will destroy you until no inhabitant is left... The remnant of the house of Judah shall pasture there; in the houses of Ashkelon they shall lie down in the **Evening**, for Jehovah their God will **Visit** them and restore their captives" (Zephaniah 2:5, 7).

**2324.** Lot, when he was with Abraham, represented the Lord’s **Sensual** nature <note>original: "Sensuale Domini"; in this context, "sensual" refers to the lowest level of the mind, which perceives the world through the physical senses</note>, and thus His External part, as was shown in Part One (numbers 1428, 1434, 1547). Now that he is separated from Abraham, he no longer represents the Lord, but instead represents those who are with the Lord—specifically the **External man of the Church** <note>original: "Externum hominem Ecclesiæ"</note>. These are the people who live in the good of charity but remain in external forms of worship. Indeed, in this chapter, Lot represents not only the External Church as it is in its beginning, but also as it progresses and reaches its end. The end of that Church is signified by **Moab and the son of Ammon** <note>original: "Moabum & Filium Ammonis"</note>, as will become clear, by the Lord's Divine Mercy, from the sequence that follows. It is common in the Word for one person to represent several successive states, which are described through the sequential acts of their life. 

Regarding the meaning of the **Gate**: a gate is that through which one enters or exits a city. Therefore, **"sitting in the gate"** signifies being among the wicked here, but still being separate from them. This is typical for people of the Church who are in the good of charity; even though they are among the wicked, they are nonetheless separated from them—not in terms of civil society, but in terms of their spiritual life. It was stated above (number 2322) that **Sodom** signifies evil in general, or the wicked, especially those within the Church.

**2325. "And Lot saw,"** which signifies **conscience** <note>original: "conscientiam"</note>—specifically the conscience of those who are in the good of charity but in external worship. This is evident from the meaning of "seeing." In the Word, "to see" signifies to understand (see numbers 897, 1584, 1806, 1807, 2150). In the **internal sense** <note>the deeper spiritual meaning beneath the literal story</note>, however, it signifies having faith; this meaning will be discussed, by the Lord’s Divine Mercy, at Verse 32 of Genesis Chapter 29. The reason it signifies "Conscience" here is that those who have faith also have conscience; the two are inseparable. In fact, they are so linked that whether you say "faith" or "conscience," it amounts to the same thing. By "faith," we mean the faith through which charity comes and which springs from charity—that is, charity itself—for faith without charity is no faith at all. And just as faith cannot exist without charity, neither can conscience.

**2326. "And he rose to meet them,"** which signifies **acknowledgment** <note>original: "agnitionem"</note> as well as an affection for charity. This is clear from the fact that when the angels arrived, Lot immediately recognized them as such. This was not the case with the men of Sodom, of whom it is said: *"They called to Lot and said, 'Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us so that we may know them'"* (Verse 5). 

In the internal sense, these words signify that those within the Church who are in the good of charity recognize the **Divine Human** and the **Holy Proceeding** of the Lord <note>original: "Divinum Humanum & Sanctum procedens Domini"; the "Holy Proceeding" refers to the Holy Spirit or the Lord's active influence</note>, who are represented by the two angels. However, those who are not in the good of charity do not recognize them. The fact that these words also involve an affection for charity is evident because Lot—who represents those in the good of charity, and indeed signifies the good of charity itself—invited them into his house.

They were unable to join these three together in their minds, but kept them separate. 

The reason for this is that every secret—even the most profound—carries an underlying mental image <note>original: "idea"</note>, for nothing can be thought of or even remembered without such an image. Therefore, in the next life, it is as clear as daylight what kind of thought and faith each person formed for themselves regarding the One God. Indeed, when the Jews in the next life hear that the Lord is Jehovah and that there is only One God, they have nothing to say against it. However, when they perceive that the ideas of Christians are divided among Three, they say they themselves worship one God, while Christians worship three. This is especially true because no one can join those Three together in their mind except those who are in the faith of charity, for the Lord connects the minds of such people to Himself.

Conversely, when ideas are held in the internal sense, the literal sense appears similarly obscure—indeed, to the angels, it is as if it were nothing. # GENESIS

To **spend the night in the street**, in the internal sense, means to judge from truth. Regarding **judgment** <note>original: "Judicium"</note>, it is twofold: namely, judgment from **good** <note>original: "bonum"</note> and judgment from **truth** <note>original: "verum"</note>. The faithful are judged from good, while the unfaithful are judged from truth. 

That the faithful are judged from good is clearly seen in Matthew chapter 25, from verses 34 to 40; and that the unfaithful are judged from truth is shown there from verses 41 to 46. To be judged from good is to be saved, because they have received it. But to be judged from truth is to be condemned, because they have rejected what is good. 

Good belongs to the Lord. Those who acknowledge this in their life and faith belong to the Lord, and therefore they are saved. But those who do not acknowledge it in their life, and consequently not in their faith, cannot belong to the Lord and thus cannot be saved. They are therefore judged according to the actions of their life and according to their thoughts and intentions. When judged by these things, they cannot help but be condemned; for it is a truth that a person, of themselves, does nothing but evil, thinks nothing but evil, and intends nothing but evil. Left to themselves, they would rush toward hell unless they were held back by the Lord. 

But this is how judgment from truth works: the Lord never judges anyone except from good. For He wishes to raise everyone, however many there are, into heaven—indeed, if He could, even to Himself. For the Lord is **Mercy** <note>original: "Misericordia"</note> itself and **Good** itself. Mercy itself and Good itself can never condemn anyone. Rather, it is the person who condemns themselves by rejecting good. Just as a person fled from good during their physical life, they continue to flee from it in the next life, and consequently they flee from heaven and the Lord. For the Lord can only be present in what is good. He is also present in truth, but never in truth that is separated from good. 

That the Lord does not condemn anyone, or judge them to hell, He says Himself in the Gospel of John: 

> "God did not send His Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through Him. This is the judgment: that Light has come into the world, but people loved darkness more than light, because their works were evil" (John 3:17, 19 <note>original: "Non misit Deus Filium suum..."</note>).

And in the same book: 

> "If anyone hears my words but does not believe, I do not judge him; for I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world" (John 12:47 <note>original: "Si quis mea audiverit verba..."</note>).

Furthermore, see what was said on this previously in numbers 223, 245, 592, 696, 1093, 1683, 1874, and 2258. Where judgment was discussed above in numbers 2320 and 2321, it was shown that all judgment belongs to the Lord’s Divine Human and the Holy Proceeding, according to the Lord’s words in John: "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son" (John 5:22 <note>original: "Non Pater judicat quemquam..."</note>). And yet, it is now said that the Lord does not judge by condemning anyone. From this, it is clear what the Word is like in its literal sense: unless it were understood through another sense—namely, the **internal sense** <term>The "internal sense" refers to the hidden, spiritual meaning of the Bible that lies beneath the literal stories and history.</term>—it would not be understood at all. Only through the internal sense does the nature of judgment become clear.

This passage refers to the Lord's coming. That the "street and trench" will be restored means that truth and good will then be present. It is well known that the physical city of Jerusalem was not restored and built at that time, and anyone can see it is not to be physically rebuilt in the future. One can understand this if they do not limit their ideas to a worldly kingdom, but instead look to the heavenly kingdom, which is what "Jerusalem" means in its internal sense. 

In Luke: "The master of the house said to his servant, 'Go out quickly into the **streets** and **lanes** <note>original: "Plateas & Vicos"</note> of the city, and bring in here the poor, the maimed, the lame, and the blind,'" Luke 14:21. Those who stay only in the literal sense of the text think this means nothing more than the servant going everywhere (signified by streets and lanes) and bringing in everyone (signified by the poor, maimed, lame, and blind). But every single word involves hidden spiritual secrets <note>original: "arcana"</note>, for these are the Lord's words. Going into the "streets and lanes" signifies seeking genuine truth wherever it may be—truth that shines from good or through which good is transparent. Bringing in the "poor, maimed, lame, and blind" signifies those who were so-called in the Ancient Church <note>original: "Antiqua Ecclesia"</note>: people who lacked faith but lived a life of good, and who were thus to be instructed about the Lord’s Kingdom. This refers to the nations (Gentiles) who had not yet been taught. 

Because "streets" signified truths, there was a symbolic ritual among the Jews of teaching in the streets, as seen in Matthew 6:2, 5 and Luke 13:26–27. 

In the Prophets <note>original: "Prophetas"</note>, whenever streets are mentioned, they signify in the internal sense either truths or things contrary to truths. For example:

*   In Isaiah: "Justice is turned back, and righteousness stands afar off; for **truth has stumbled in the street**, and **uprightness** cannot enter," Isaiah 59:14. 
*   In the same prophet: "Your sons have fainted; they lie at the head of **all the streets**," Isaiah 51:20. 
*   In Jeremiah: "Death has come up into our windows, it has entered our palaces, to cut off the child from the **street**, and the young men from the **lanes**," Jeremiah 9:21. 
*   In Ezekiel: "With the hooves of his horses Nebuchadnezzar shall trample all **your streets**," Ezekiel 26:11. This refers to Tyre, which signifies the knowledge of truth (see number 1201). The "hooves of the horses" are the external facts <note>original: "scientifica"</note> that pervert the truth. 
*   In Nahum: "The chariots rage in the **streets**, they jostle one another in the lanes," Nahum 2:4. "Chariots" represent the doctrine of truth, which are said to "rage in the streets" when falsehood is accepted in place of truth. 
*   In Zechariah: "Old men and old women shall again dwell in the **streets** of Jerusalem, and the **streets** of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in the **streets**," Zechariah 8:4–5. This refers to the affection for truth, and the resulting joys and happiness. 

This meaning also appears elsewhere, such as in Isaiah 24:11; Jeremiah 5:1, 7:34, 49:26; Lamentations 2:11, 4:8, 14; and Zephaniah 3:6.

# GENESIS.

2337. **Verse 3: *And he urged them strongly, and they turned aside to him, and they came into his house; and he made them a feast, and baked unleavened bread, and they ate.*** <note>original: "Et urgebat eos valde, & declinaverunt ad eum, & venerunt ad domum ejus, & fecit eis convivium, & azyma coxit, & comederunt."</note> **He urged them strongly** signifies a state of temptation when a person overcomes it. **And they turned aside to him** signifies staying or abiding. **And they came into his house** signifies being confirmed in what is good. **And he made them a feast** <note>original: "convivium"</note> signifies dwelling together. **And he baked unleavened bread** signifies purification. **And they ate** signifies appropriation <note>term: appropriation — the process of making spiritual truths and goodness a permanent part of one's own life and character.</note>.

2338. **He urged them strongly**, which signifies a state of temptation when a person overcomes, can only be understood by those who have experienced spiritual temptations. As previously mentioned, temptations involve doubts about the Lord's presence and mercy, as well as doubts regarding one's own salvation. The evil spirits who are present with a person at that time and who trigger the temptation strongly inspire a negative viewpoint. However, the good spirits and angels from the Lord dispel this doubt in every possible way, keeping the person constantly in hope and ultimately confirming a positive or "affirmative" state. 

Consequently, a person in temptation hangs in the balance between the negative and the affirmative. One who gives in remains in doubt and falls into the negative. But one who overcomes is indeed in doubt, yet allows themselves to be raised up by hope and persists in the affirmative. Because in that struggle the person seems to "urge" the Lord—especially through prayers—to be present, to have mercy, to bring help, and to deliver them from spiritual ruin. Here, where the text describes the temptation of those who are becoming members of the Church, it is described by the fact that the Angels first said "no" and intended to stay in the street all night, but that Lot urged them strongly, and so they turned aside to him and entered his house.

2339. **And they turned aside to him**, which signifies staying or abiding, is clear from the meaning of the same words used above in section 2330, and so requires no further explanation.

2340. **And they came into his house**, which signifies being confirmed in what is good, is established by the meaning of a "house" as celestial good <note>original: "coeleste bonum"</note>, as discussed previously in sections 2234 and 2331. Therefore, according to the internal sequence of the subject matter, it means being confirmed in that good.

2341. **And he made them a feast**, which signifies dwelling together <note>original: "cohabitationem"</note>, is clear from the meaning of a "feast." Feasts are mentioned frequently in the Word, and in the internal sense, they signify dwelling together. For example, in Jeremiah: "The word of Jehovah came to him: *You shall not enter the house of feasting, to sit with them, to eat and to drink*" (Jeremiah 16:8). Here, many things are said to the Prophet to represent that good has no communication with evil, and truth has no communication with falsehood; among these, he was told not to enter a "house of feasting," which signified that good and truth would not dwell together with evil and falsehood. 

In Isaiah: "On this mountain, Jehovah of Hosts <note>original: "Jehovah Zebaoth"</note> will make for all people a **feast of rich foods** <note>original: "pinguium," literally "fat things"</note>, a **feast of sweet wines**, of rich foods full of marrow, of refined wines" (Isaiah 25:6). In this passage, "Mountain" represents love for the Lord (see sections 795, 1430). Those who are in this love dwell with the Lord in good and truth, which is signified by the "feast." The "rich foods" and "marrow" are goods (section 353), and the "sweet and refined wines" are the truths derived from them (section 1071). The feasts made from consecrated things when they sacrificed in the Jewish Church meant nothing else...

# CHAPTER NINETEEN.

...they represented the Lord living together with humanity in the holy things of love signified by sacrifices (number 2187). It was the same later with the Holy Supper, which in the early Church was called a **Banquet** <note>original: *Convivium*</note>. In Genesis 21:7, it is mentioned that Abraham made a great feast on the day Isaac was weaned. This represented and signified the living together and the first union <note>original: *conjunctio*</note> of the Divine Lord with His **Human Rational** <term>Human Rational: the intermediate part of the mind where human reason meets spiritual influence.</term>. The same is signified by banquets in other places in the internal sense. This can be concluded from the fact that banquets occur among many people who are together in love and charity, who join their minds together and mutually share their joys—which are the feelings of love and charity.

2342. **And he baked unleavened bread**, which signifies purification, is clear from the meaning of "unleavened" <note>original: *azyma*</note> or unfermented. Throughout the Word, **Bread** generally signifies all heavenly and spiritual food, and thus all heavenly and spiritual things in general (see numbers 276, 680, 1798, 2165, 2177). To show that these should be free from impurities, they were represented by **unleavened bread**. This is because **leaven** <note>original: *fermentum*</note> signifies evil and falsity, which make heavenly and spiritual things impure and profane. 

Because of this representation, those in the Representative Church <term>Representative Church: an era of spiritual history where outward rituals were used to represent internal, heavenly realities.</term> were commanded not to offer any bread in their sacrifices—specifically the **grain offering** <note>original: *mincha*</note>—that was fermented or leavened. This is clear in the writings of Moses: **"Every grain offering which you bring to the Lord shall not be made with leaven"** (Leviticus 2:11). Elsewhere: **"You shall not sacrifice the blood of my sacrifice with leavened bread"** (Exodus 23:18; 34:25). 

For this reason, it was also commanded that during the seven days of the **Passover**, they should eat no bread other than unfermented or unleavened bread. Moses writes: **"For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread; even on the first day you shall remove leaven from your houses. For whoever eats anything leavened from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel... On the fourteenth day of the month at evening, you shall eat unleavened bread, until the twenty-first day of the month at evening. For seven days no leaven shall be found in your houses, for whoever eats what is leavened, that soul shall be cut off from the congregation of Israel, whether he is a stranger or a native of the land"** (Exodus 12:15, 18, 19, 20; see also Exodus 13:6, 7; 23:15; 34:18; Deuteronomy 16:3, 4). Because of this, the Passover is called the **Feast of Unleavened Bread** (Leviticus 23:6; Numbers 28:16, 17; Matthew 26:17; Luke 22:1, 7). 

That the Passover represented the **Glorification of the Lord**, and thus the union of the Divine with the human race, will be shown elsewhere by the Lord's Divine Mercy. Because the Lord’s union with the human race happens through love and charity (and through the faith that comes from them), these heavenly and spiritual things were represented by the unleavened bread eaten during the Passover. To prevent these things from being contaminated by anything profane, leaven was so strictly forbidden that anyone who ate it was to be "cut off." Those who profane heavenly and spiritual things cannot help but perish. Anyone can see that without this hidden meaning <note>original: *arcanum*</note>, such a ceremonial law with such a severe penalty would never have been enacted. Everything commanded in that Church represented a hidden spiritual reality—even the act of baking itself.

# GENESIS.

...every single thing they did when the children of Israel left Egypt, namely: 
“That they should eat the meat that night, roasted with fire, and **unleavened bread** <note>original: *Azyma*</note> with bitter herbs; they should not eat it raw, nor boiled in water; the head with the legs; that they should leave none of it until morning, but burn the remainder with fire” (Exodus 12:8–10). Every one of these details was representative: eating at night, the meat roasted with fire, the unleavened bread with bitter herbs, the head with the legs, not raw, not boiled in water, leaving nothing until morning, and burning the rest. However, these secrets are never apparent unless revealed through the **internal sense** <term>internal sense: the deeper, spiritual meaning of the Bible that lies beneath the literal stories and laws.</term>. It is only from this sense that it becomes clear how everything in the Word is Divine. 

The same is true for the ritual of the **Nazirite** <term>Nazirite: a person in the Old Testament who took a special vow of devotion to God, often involving not cutting their hair.</term>: “The priest shall take the boiled shoulder of the ram, and one unleavened cake from the basket, and one unleavened wafer, and shall put them upon the hands of the Nazirite after he has shaved the hair of his separation” (Numbers 6:19). Anyone who does not know that the Nazirite represented the **celestial man** <note>original: *coelestem hominem*; a person who acts from a state of pure love rather than just duty or faith</note> himself also does not know that every single one of these details involves heavenly things—secrets that do not appear in the literal text—such as the boiled shoulder of the ram, the unleavened cake, the unleavened wafer, and the shaving of the hair. 

From this, one can see what kind of opinion those who do not believe in an internal sense might have of the Word; for without the internal meaning, these details are of no importance. But when the ceremonial or ritual aspect is removed, everything there becomes Divine and Holy. This is also the case with **unleavened bread** <note>original: *Azymo*</note>, which is the "holy thing of love," or the "holy of holies," as it is also called in the books of Moses: “The **unleavened bread** <note>original: *Azyma*</note> that remains shall be eaten by Aaron and his sons in a holy place, because it is the holy of holies” (Leviticus 6:16–17) <note>original reference says Lev 6:9-10, corresponding to the Latin Vulgate numbering</note>. Therefore, unleavened bread is pure love, and the baking of unleavened bread is **purification** <note>original: *purificatio*</note>.

2343. **And they ate**, which signifies **appropriation** <term>appropriation: the process by which a person makes spiritual truths and goodness a permanent part of their own life and character.</term>, is evident from the meaning of "eating," which is to be communicated with and joined, and thus to be appropriated (as discussed previously in number 2187). 

From what has now been said and explained, it is clear how the details contained in the previous verse and this one hold together in the internal sense:
* By the **Angels** is signified the **Divine Human** <note>original: *Divinum Humanum*</note> and the Holy proceeding from the Lord.
* By **turning aside to him** is signified having a dwelling place.
* By **coming to his house** is signified being confirmed in what is good.
* By **making a feast** is signified living together.
* By **baking unleavened bread** is signified being purified.
* By **eating** is signified being appropriated.

From this, the sequence of things in the internal sense is clear, even though none of it appears in the historical sense. Such is the order and series in every part of the Word. However, the sequence itself cannot shine forth in the explanation of individual words, for then they appear as separate things, and the continuity of the meaning is broken. But when all things are viewed together in a single idea, or perceived in one intuition of thought—as happens with those who are in the internal sense and simultaneously in heavenly light from the Lord—the entire process of **reformation and regeneration** <term>regeneration: the spiritual process of being reborn or made new by God.</term> of those who become people of the Church (represented here by Lot) is presented to be seen in those words. 

Namely: that they first perceive something of temptation; but when they persist and overcome, the Lord has a dwelling place with them, confirms them in what is good, introduces them into His Kingdom to Himself, lives with them, and there purifies and perfects them, and at the same time makes goodness their own.

# CHAPTER NINETEEN

...[unleavened cakes are] good and happy things, and this through His **Divine Human** <note>original: *Divinum Humanum*; the concept of God's nature being both Divine and Human</note> and the Holy proceeding from Him. For those who are not in this state, it is as impossible to believe this as it is for a camel to go through the eye of a needle. This is because the good of charity is the very soil for the seeds of faith. Truth and good agree, but truth and evil never do; they are of opposite natures, and one turns away from the other. Therefore, as much as a person is in good, so much can they be in truth—or as much as they are in charity, so much are they in faith—especially in this primary principle of faith: that all salvation comes from the Lord.

And also: “I am the vine, you are the branches. He who remains in Me, and I in him, bears much fruit; for without Me you can do nothing. This is my commandment, that *you love one another as I have loved you*” (John 15:5, 6, 9, 12).

From these passages, it is clear that love for the Lord and charity toward the neighbor are the life of faith. However, those who are in evil—that is, in a life of evil—can never believe that all salvation is from the Lord. I have seen this clearly from those who have come into the next life from the Christian world, even those who, during their bodily life, confessed with their mouths (and even taught according to the doctrine of faith) that there is no salvation without the Lord, yet lived a life of evil. This was of such a nature that it extinguished, suffocated, and perverted every perception of love for the Lord...

# G E N E S I S.

...[love for] God and charity toward one’s neighbor. Such is the faith today that people claim saves even without the "goods" of charity. Truth cannot flow from any source other than the Lord, nor can truth be sown except in the **good** <term>good: in this context, the spiritual state of acting out of love and kindness, which serves as fertile "soil" for faith.</term> that comes from the Lord.

That the **Divine Human** <note>original: *Humanum Divinum*; the concept of God's nature being both Divine and Human</note> and the "Holy proceeding" from the Lord are the source of life and salvation is clearly known from the words of the **Holy Supper** <note>original: *Sacræ Cœnæ*; the ritual of Communion or the Eucharist</note>: "This is my Body, This is my Blood." It is evident that the Lord's Divine Human is the source of everything Holy. 2344. **Verse 4.** *They had hardly yet lain down, when the men of the city, the men of Sodom, surrounded the house, from the boy even to the old man, all the people from the farthest end.*
"They had hardly yet lain down" signifies the first time of **visitation** <term>visitation: a period of spiritual exploration or judgment where the true state of a person or a church is revealed.</term>. "All the people from the farthest end" signifies every single one of them.

2345. "They had hardly yet lain down" signifies the first time of visitation. This is clear from what was said above regarding "Evening" and "Night" (in sections 2323 and 2325)—namely, that in the **Word** <note>original: *Verbo*; the Bible</note>, these terms signify Visitation and Judgment. While "evening" or "night" is not specifically named here, the phrase "hardly yet lain down" is used, which signifies the time when evening is passing into night, or the beginning of night. Consequently, it refers to the first time of visitation upon evils, as is also clear from what follows; for here begins the inquiry into the evils within the Church (represented here by Sodom).

2346. "The men of the city" signifies those in falsities, and "the men of Sodom" signifies those in evils. This is clear from the meaning of "City" and "Sodom." It was shown previously (in section 402) that a "City" signifies truths, as well as falsities (the opposites of truth), and that "Sodom" signifies every kind of evil (sections 2220, 2246). Because both falsities and evils were being examined or "visited," the text says "men of the city" and "men of Sodom." If both were not intended, it would have only said "the men of Sodom."

2347. "Surrounded the house" signifies being against the good of charity. This is clear from the meaning of "House," which represents **celestial good** <term>celestial good: the highest form of spiritual goodness, rooted in love for the Lord and others.</term> (which is nothing other than the good of love and charity, as seen in sections 2048 and 2234). It is also clear from the meaning of "surrounding," which is to be against something, or to attack and oppose it with hostile intent.

# CHAPTER NINETEEN.

2348. **From the boy even to the old man** <note>original: *A puero & usque ad senem*</note>. That this signifies falsities and evils—both those that are recent and those that are firmly established—can be established from the meaning of "Boy" and "Old Man" when they are used to describe falsities and evils. "Boys" represent things that have not yet matured, and are therefore **recent**. "Old men" represent things that have reached a great age, and are therefore **confirmed** or long-held. Elsewhere in the Word <note>The "Word" refers to the Bible</note>, "boy" and "old man" occur with a similar meaning, as in Zechariah:

> "There shall yet dwell **old men** and **old women** in the streets of Jerusalem, and the streets of the city shall be filled with **boys** and **girls** playing in the streets" (Zechariah 8:4, 5).

In this passage, **Jerusalem** stands for the Lord’s Kingdom and the Church; **streets** stand for the truths found there. Thus, **old men** represent confirmed truths, and **old women** represent confirmed "goods" <term>goods: the spiritual quality of love and kindness</term>. **Boys** playing in the streets represent recent truths, and **girls** represent recent "goods" and the affection and joy that come from them. 

From this, it is clear how heavenly and spiritual things are transformed into historical stories when they descend into the worldly matters that make up the literal sense of the Bible. In that literal sense, it hardly appears as anything other than a description of actual old men, boys, women, and girls. 

Similarly, in Jeremiah: 

> "Pour out upon the **child** in the street of Jerusalem, and upon the assembly of young men likewise; for even the husband with the wife shall be taken, the **old man** with him who is full of days" (Jeremiah 6:11). 

Here, the **street of Jerusalem** represents the falsities that rule in the Church. The recent and adult versions of these are called the **child** and **young men**, while the ancient and confirmed versions are called the **old man** and the **one full of days**. 

Also in Jeremiah: 

> "I will scatter in you the horse and his rider, and I will scatter in you the chariot and him that is carried in it, and I will scatter in you man and woman, and I will scatter in you **old man and boy**" (Jeremiah 51:21, 22). 

In this context, **old man and boy** similarly represent confirmed and recent truth. 

Again in Jeremiah: 

> "Death has climbed into the windows, it has come into our palaces, to cut off the **child** in the street, the **young men** from the lanes" (Jeremiah 9:20). 

In this case, the **child** represents truths that are just being born, which are cut off when "death" enters the **windows** and **palaces**—that is, the **intellectual** and **voluntary** <term>voluntary: the part of the human mind related to the will or desires</term> parts of a person. That "windows" represent intellectual things, see note 655 and 658; that "palaces" or "houses" represent the things of the will, see note 710.

2349. **All the people from the end** <note>original: *Omnis populus ab extremo*; often translated as "from every quarter"</note>. That this signifies each and every one of them is clear from what precedes. Since "boys and old men" signify both recent and confirmed falsities and evils, "all the people from the end" now refers to every single one of them. In a general sense, **people** also signifies falsities (see notes 1259, 1260). 

Here is described the first state of those within the Church who are against the "good" of charity and, consequently, against the Lord. For one involves the other; no one can be joined to the Lord except through love and charity. Love is the actual spiritual connection, as is clear from the very nature of love. Anyone who cannot be joined to the Lord cannot acknowledge Him either. That those who are not in "good" cannot acknowledge the Lord—that is, cannot have faith in Him—is clear in the Gospel of John:

> "Light has come into the world, but men loved darkness rather than Light, **for their works were evil**. For everyone who does evil hates the Light, and does not come to the Light, lest **his** works should be reproved. But he who does the truth comes to the Light, so that **his** works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God" (John 3:19, 20, 21).

From these words, it is clear that those who are against the "good" of charity are against...

Similarly, it says elsewhere in the same book, "The world cannot hate you, but it hates Me, because I testify of it, that its works are evil" (John 7:7). This is even more evident in Matthew: 

> "He will say to those on His left hand, 'Depart from Me, you cursed; for I was hungry and you gave Me nothing to eat; I was thirsty and you gave Me no drink; I was a stranger and you did not take Me in; naked and you did not clothe Me; sick and in prison and you did not visit Me. From this it is clear how those who are against the "good" of charity <term>charity: the spiritual love of one's neighbor</term> are against the Lord. It also shows that everyone is judged according to the "good" that comes from charity, not according to the "truth" of faith when that faith is separated from good. As it says elsewhere in Matthew: "The Son of Man shall come in the glory of His Father with His angels, and then He shall reward every man according to his deeds" (Matthew 16:27). "Deeds" <note>original: *facta*</note> refer to the good things that proceed from charity; these are called the "fruits of faith."

***

2350. **Verse 5. *And they called out to Lot and said to him, "Where are the men who came to you tonight? Bring them out to us, so that we may know them."*** 

**They called out to Lot and said to him** signifies falsity stemming from evil, raging against what is good. **Where are the men who came to you** signifies a denial of the Lord’s Divine Human <term>Divine Human: The theological concept that God took on a human form in order to reach and save humanity</term> and the Holy Spirit proceeding from Him. **Tonight** <note>original: *noctu*</note> signifies the final time when these things are no longer recognized. **Bring them out to us, so that we may know them** signifies that they wanted to show it is false to acknowledge that these Divine qualities even exist.

2351. **They called out to Lot and said to him.** That this signifies falsity from evil raging against good can be established from the meaning of "calling out" and the representation of Lot, as well as the emotion behind the words. It has been shown previously (n. 2240) that the word "calling out" <note>original: *clamare*</note> is used in relation to falsity. Lot represents the people of the Church who are "in good" <term>in good: living a life characterized by love and moral integrity</term>, and thus represents good itself (n. 2324). From this, and from the atmosphere of anger in these words, it is clear that this signifies falsity from evil raging against good. 

There are several kinds of falsity, but generally there are two: falsity that is produced *from* evil, and falsity that *produces* evil (see n. 1188, 1212, 1295, 1679, 2243). The falsity from evil that exists within the Church is primarily the kind that encourages a wicked life. For example, the idea that "good" (charity) does not make a person a member of the Church, but only "truth" (faith) does; or that a person can be saved regardless of how wickedly they have lived their whole life, provided that—shortly before death, while their bodily senses are fading—they utter some statement of faith with an appearance of affection. This specific falsity is what rages most against "good," and it is signified by the people calling out to Lot. 

The cause of anger is anything that tries to destroy the delight of a person's love. It is called **Anger** when evil attacks good, but it is called **Zeal** when good rebukes evil.

2352. **Where are the men who came to you.** That this signifies the denial of the Lord's Divine Human and the Holy proceeding <note>original: *Sancti procedentis*</note> is evident from the significance of the "two men" (discussed above in n. 2320), and also from the tone of anger in these words.

2353. **At night**, which signifies the final time when things are no longer recognized. This is evident from the meaning of "Night" as a time of darkness, when things belonging to the light can no longer be seen. The angels did not come at night, but in the evening; however, because these are the men of Sodom speaking and shouting—that is, people who are in falsity and evil—it is not called "evening" but "night." In the Word <term>the Word: a term for the Holy Scriptures or Bible</term>, "Night" signifies a time and state when there is no longer any light of truth, but only falsity and evil; thus, it refers to the final stage when judgment occurs. This meaning appears frequently, as in Micah: 

> "Against the prophets who lead the people astray: **Night** shall come to you without a vision, and it shall grow dark for you without divination; the sun shall set on the prophets, and the day shall turn black over them" (<term>III</term>: 5-6). 

"Prophets" here refers to those who teach falsities; "night," "growing dark," the "setting of the sun," and the "blackening day" refer to falsities and evils. In John: "If anyone walks in the day, he does not stumble; but if anyone walks in the **Night**, he stumbles, because the light is not in him" (<term>XI</term>: 9-10); where "night" stands for falsity stemming from evil, and "light" for truth stemming from good. For just as all light of truth comes from what is good, all night of falsity comes from what is evil. In the same book: "I must work the works of Him who sent Me while it is day; the **Night** comes when no one can work" (<term>IX</term>: 4); "day" stands for the time and state when there is good and truth, while "night" stands for when there is evil and falsity. In Luke: "I tell you, in that **Night** there will be two in one bed; one will be accepted, and the other will be left behind" (<term>XVII</term>: 34). Here "night" refers to the final time, when the truth of faith no longer exists. 

Because the devastation <term>devastation: a spiritual state where all truth and goodness have been lost</term> of good and truth within the Church was represented in Egypt when the children of Israel were leaving—and because nothing but falsity and evil reigned there anymore—it was commanded that they should leave at *midnight* (Exodus <term>XI</term>: 4). It also happened that at *midnight* all the firstborn of Egypt were killed (Exodus <term>XII</term>: 12, 29, 30). And because those who are in good and truth (represented by the Children of Israel) were guarded among those falsities and evils—just as Lot was in Sodom—that night, in respect to them, is called the **"Night of the Lord's keeping"** <note>original: *Nox cuftodiarum Jehovæ*</note> (Exodus 12:42).

2354. This is evident from the meaning of the two angels (mentioned above in section 2320), and also from the feeling of anger in which these words were spoken, which implies a denial. 

This describes the first state of a "devastated" Church—that is, when faith begins to vanish because there is no charity. ...for the sake of dishonest gain. They worship Him outwardly in a holy manner, but inwardly they hide that which is profane. As has been mentioned several times before, every person has both evil spirits and angels present with them. Through evil spirits, a person communicates with hell, and through angels, they communicate with heaven (see sections 687, 697). Therefore, as much as someone's life moves toward evil, hell flows into them; but as much as their life moves toward good, heaven flows into them, and thus the Lord. From this, it is clear that those who live an evil life cannot acknowledge the Lord; instead, they invent countless arguments against Him because they receive the fantasies of hell that flow into them. But those who live a good life acknowledge the Lord because heaven flows into them—a heaven in which love and charity <term>charity: spiritual love for one's neighbor</term> are the principal things. This is because heaven belongs to the Lord, from whom all things of love and charity originate (see sections 537, 540, 547, 548, 551, 553, 685, 2130).

2355. **Verses 6, 7. *And Lot went out to them to the doorway, and shut the door after him. And he said, "I beg you, my brothers, do not act wickedly."***
"Lot went out to them to the doorway" signifies that he applied himself to them with prudence. "And shut the door after him" signifies that they should not violate the "good" of charity or deny the **Divine Human** <term>Divine Human: The theological concept that the Lord's humanity is itself Divine</term> and the Holy Proceeding of the Lord. "And he said" signifies an exhortation. "I beg you, my brothers, do not act wickedly" signifies that they should not violate those holy things. He calls them "brothers" because he was speaking from a state of "good," which was the basis of his exhortation.

2356. The fact that "going out to the doorway" signifies that he applied himself prudently is evident from the internal meaning of a **Doorway** <note>original Latin: *Janua*</note> and "going out to the doorway." In the Word <term>the Word: Holy Scripture</term>, a "doorway" signifies that which introduces or admits one to either Truth, or Good, or to the Lord Himself. For this reason, a doorway also signifies Truth itself, Good itself, and the Lord Himself; for Truth leads to Good, and Good leads to the Lord. Such things were represented by the doorways and curtains of the Tabernacle, as well as those of the Temple (see sections 2145, 2152, 2576). That this is the meaning of a doorway is clear from the Lord's words in John: 

> "**Truly, truly, I say to you, he** who does not enter the sheepfold by the **Doorway**, but climbs up some other way, is a thief and a robber; but he who enters by the **Doorway** is the shepherd of the sheep; to him the gatekeeper opens... I am the **Doorway** of the sheep; if anyone enters through Me, he will be saved" (10:1–3, 7, 9). 

In this passage, "doorway" stands for Truth and Good, and thus for the Lord, who is Truth and Good itself. From this, it is clear what is signified by being "admitted through the doorway into heaven," and consequently, what is meant by the "keys" with which it is opened. 

In this specific context, however, "doorway" signifies a certain "good" that was adapted to the nature <note>original: *genio*</note> of those who were besieging the house. Here, the "doorway" <note>original: *janua*</note> is distinguished from the physical "door" <note>original: *ostium*</note>, and it was in front of the house. This is clear from the fact that Lot "went out" and then "shut the door after him." That this good was the happiness of life is evident from what follows immediately, by which he hoped to persuade those who were in falsity and evil. Such people do not allow themselves to be persuaded by "good" in its truest sense, for they reject it. From these points, it is clear that "going out to the doorway" signifies that he applied himself to them with prudence.

2357. **And shut the door after him**, which signifies that they should not violate the good of charity or deny the Divine Human and the Holy Proceeding of the Lord, is evident from what has just been said. To "close the door" is to prevent them from entering—in this case, preventing them from entering into "good"...

This is because of the punishment for profanation, which is most severe in hell. This is why so few today are granted the ability to believe from the heart that the "good" of love and charity is the heaven within a person, and that all things Divine are in the Lord; for people are generally living in evil. This is the interior meaning of why Lot "shut the door after him." The door was the inner entrance through which one entered into the house where the angels were—that is, into the state of "good" where the Lord resides.

2358. **And he said**: This signifies an **exhortation** <term>exhortation: a strong urging or pleading</term>, as is clear from the words that follow; therefore, no further explanation is needed.

2359. **I beg you, my brothers, do not act wickedly**: This signifies that they should not violate those things—namely, the "good" of charity and the **Divine Human** <term>Divine Human: The concept that the Lord’s humanity is fully Divine and the source of all holiness</term> and the Holy proceeding from the Lord. This is clear from the meaning of "acting wickedly," which is to violate. From this, it is evident that this passage concerns those within the Church, and that these are the people understood by the "men of Sodom." No one can violate these holy things except those who possess the **Word** <term>the Word: the Holy Scriptures or Divine revelation</term>. 

That these things are most holy is evident from the fact that no one can be admitted into the Lord's Kingdom—that is, into Heaven—unless they are in the "good" of love and charity. Furthermore, no one can be in the "good" of love and charity unless they acknowledge the Lord's Divine and Holy nature. All "good" flows from Him alone, and specifically into the "good" that comes from Him. The Divine can only flow into what is Divine, and it cannot be communicated to a human except through the **Divine Human**, and the holiness that comes from it. From this, one can understand why the Lord is "all in all" in His Kingdom, and why nothing of the "good" found in a human belongs to the human, but rather to the Lord.

2360. The reason he calls them **brothers** is that he is speaking from the "good" from which he exhorted them. This is clear from the meaning of "brother." In the Word, "brother" means the same as "neighbor," because everyone should love their neighbor as themselves. Thus, they are called "brothers" out of love, or (which is the same thing) out of "good." 

This naming and greeting of one's neighbor comes from the fact that in Heaven, the Lord is the Father of all, and He loves everyone as His children. Thus, love is the spiritual bond that joins everyone together. Consequently, the whole of heaven is like one single family <note>original: "generationem"</note> born of love and charity (see sections 685, 917). For this reason, all the children of Israel—because they represented the Lord’s heavenly Kingdom of love and charity—called each other "Brothers." They were also called "Companions," but this term "companions" did not refer to the "good" of love, but rather to the "truth" of faith. As it says in Isaiah: *"A man helps his **companion**, and says to his **brother**, 'Be strong!'"* (41:6). And in Jeremiah: *"Thus you shall say, everyone to his **companion**, and everyone to his **brother**, 'What has the Lord answered?...'"*

## Paragraph 2361
**Verse 8: Look now, I have two daughters who have not known a man; let me, I pray, bring them out to you, and you may do to them as is good in your eyes; only do nothing to these men, because for this reason they have come under the shadow of my roof-beam.**

"And you may do to them as is good in your eyes" signifies the enjoyment they would perceive from "good." ## Paragraph 2362

In Zechariah: "Rejoice greatly, O **Daughter of Zion**; shout, O **Daughter of Jerusalem**; behold, your King comes to you" <term>Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 21:5; John 12:15</term>.

# GENESIS

...of Jerusalem, <term>Lamentations 2:15</term>. In the first part of this work, the nature of each Church—both the Heavenly and the earthly—has been discussed several times. The Heavenly Church, because it exists from love for the Lord and love toward the neighbor, is primarily likened to an unmarried daughter or a virgin. Indeed, she is even called a virgin, as in John: **"These are those who were not defiled with women, for they are virgins; these are those who follow the Lamb wherever He goes; for they are blameless before the throne of God"** <term>Revelation 14:4–5</term>. To represent this in the Jewish Church, priests were commanded not to take widows as wives, but virgins <term>Leviticus 21:13–15, Ezekiel 44:22</term>. From these things in this verse, it can be established how pure the Word is in its internal sense, even though it appears differently in the literal text. For when these words are read: **"Look, I pray, I have two daughters who have not known a man; let me, I pray, bring them out to you, and you may do to them as is good in your eyes; only do nothing to these men,"** an impure idea enters the minds of those who live in evil. Yet how chaste these things are in the internal sense is clear from the explanation: namely, that they signify the affections for good and truth, and the happiness those people would perceive from enjoying them—those who do not violate the Divine and Holy nature of the Lord.

### Paragraph 2363
**"Let me, I pray, bring them out to you"** signifies the happiness <note>original Latin: "beatitudinem"</note> derived from them—namely, from the affections for good and truth. This is established from the meaning of those words when they are applied to the "affections" <note>the emotional or spiritual leanings toward what is right and true</note>, which are represented here by the "daughters." 

As for the matter itself—namely, that happiness and joy exist only in the affection for good and truth—all those who are in evil and its pleasures are profoundly ignorant. To them, happiness in the affection for good and truth appears either as nothing at all, or as something sad, and to some even as something painful or even deadly. Infernal geniuses and spirits are of this nature; they think and believe that if the pleasure of the love of self and the world (and consequently the evils that come from it) were taken away, no life would remain for them. 

But when it is shown to them that true life, with its joy and happiness, only begins then, they feel a certain sadness at the loss of their own pleasure. When they are brought among those who live in such a heavenly life, pain and torment seize them. Furthermore, they then begin to sense within themselves something corpse-like and a dreadful hellishness. Therefore, they call heaven—where that joy and happiness reside—their "hell," and they flee as far as they can to remove and hide themselves from the face of the Lord. 

Nevertheless, it remains true that all joy and happiness consist in the affection for good (which belongs to love and charity) and the affection for truth (which belongs to faith), to the degree that truth leads to good. This is clear because heaven—that is, the angelic life—consists in this, and because it affects the innermost parts of being, flowing in from the Lord (see numbers 540, 541, and 545). Then wisdom and intelligence enter and fill the inner recesses of the mind, igniting "good" with a heavenly flame and "truth" with a heavenly light. This comes with a perception of joy and happiness that can only be described as ineffable <note>too great or extreme to be expressed or described in words</note>. Those who are in this state perceive how empty, sad, and lamentable the life of those who are in the evils of the love of self and the world really is. But so that a person may know what this life is like by comparison—namely, the life of the love of self and the world, or what is the same thing, the life of pride, greed, and envy...

It contrasts the ineffable joy of heavenly life with the miserable, "corpse-like" state of those driven by self-love and worldly desires.</summary>

...of envy, hatred, revenge, ruthlessness, or adultery. If anyone who possesses some talent of mind should create for themselves a character-sketch of any of these—or if they can, depict it before themselves based on the ideas they can grasp from experience, science, and reason—they will see, as they begin to describe or paint it, how horrible these things are. They would see that these are diabolical forms in which there is nothing human. After death, all those who find the pleasure of their life in such things become these types of forms; and they become even more horrible the more pleasure they took in them. 

Conversely, if one creates a character-sketch of love and charity, or expresses it through a form, they will see (as they describe or draw it) that it is an angelic form, full of blessed and beautiful things, containing what is heavenly and Divine. Can anyone believe that these two forms can exist together? Or that one can strip off that diabolical form and be rewritten into a form of charity simply through a "faith" to which their actual life is contrary? For after death, the life (or what is the same, the <term>affection</term> <note>original: "affectio"; in this context, the deep-seated emotional state or desire that drives a person</note>) remains with everyone. Every thought then follows this affection; therefore, the faith manifests itself exactly as it truly was in the heart.

### Paragraph 2364
**"And do to them as is good in your eyes"** signifies enjoyment according to the amount of good. This is clear from the meaning of the words and the context, as they are spoken regarding the affections signified by the daughters. The fact that he applied himself prudently was signified by Lot going out to them to the door (no. 2356). This prudence is evident from these words and the rest of this verse: namely, that they should enjoy the happiness of the affections for good and truth according to the amount of good, which is signified by "doing to them as is good in their eyes." 

To "enjoy according to the amount of good" here means as much as they know to be good; no one is obligated beyond that. For everyone is led by the Lord toward the good of life through the good of their faith. In this way, non-Christians are led differently than Christians, the simple differently than the learned, and children differently than adults. Those who have filled their lives with evil are led by being brought to abstain from evil and intend good, doing this according to their understanding. Their intention or <term>end</term> <note>original: "finis"; the underlying purpose or goal of an action</note> is what is looked at then; and even if their actions are not good in themselves, they still draw something of good and thus of life from their intention, which constitutes their happiness.

### Paragraph 2365
**"Only do nothing to these men"** signifies that they should not violate the <term>Divine Human</term> <note>The "Divine Human" refers to the concept of God in human form, specifically Jesus Christ, as the bridge between the infinite and humanity</note> and the Holy Proceeding of the Lord. This is established from the meaning of "men" and "angels" mentioned above.

### Paragraph 2366
**"For they have come under the shadow of my roof-beam"** signifies that they are in the good of charity. This is established from the meaning of a "house" as "good" (no. 710, 2233, 2234), which is here called the "shadow of the beam" for a reason explained below.

### Paragraph 2367
As for the **"shadow of the beam"** representing a general obscurity, the situation is this: the perception of good and truth exists only in obscurity for a human being, even one who is <term>regenerated</term> <note>spiritually reborn or transformed</note>. This is even more true for someone in external worship, who is represented here by Lot. Affections, like perceptions, are very general—and therefore very obscure—when a person is in "corporeals" (that is, while living in the physical body). Although a person thinks otherwise, there are myriads upon myriads of factors in every single tiny affection, and even in every single idea of their perception, which just as...

# GENESIS

It appears as a single thing to him, which—by the Lord's Divine Mercy <note>original: "Divina Domini Misericordia"</note>—will be shown when we discuss the nature of affections and ideas. Through reflection, a person can sometimes explore and describe a few of the things within themselves. However, countless, even infinite things lie hidden, which never come to their knowledge—nor can they—as long as they live in the physical body. These things only become open after bodily and worldly concerns are extinguished. 

This is quite clear from the fact that a person who has lived in the good of love and charity <note>original: "bono amoris & charitatis"</note>, when they pass into the next life, moves from an obscure life into a clearer one, like moving from night into day. The further they enter the Lord’s heaven, the clearer it becomes, reaching the light of the Angels, whose light of intelligence and wisdom is beyond words <note>original: "ineffabilis"</note>. By comparison, the light in which humans currently live is like darkness. Thus, it says here that they **"came under the shadow of his roof,"** signifying that they are in their general obscurity—meaning that they know very little about the Divine and Holy nature of the Lord. Yet, they still acknowledge it and have faith that it exists and resides in the "good of charity"—that is, among those who live in that good.

### Paragraph 2368
**Verse 9: "And they said, 'Stand back!' and they said, 'This one man came to stay among us as a visitor, and will he act as a judge? Now we will deal worse with you than with them.' And they pressed hard against the man, against Lot, and they came near to break down the door."**

*   **And they said** signifies a response born of anger.
*   **Stand back** <note>original: "accede ultra"</note> signifies the threats of their anger.
*   **And they said, "This one man came to stay among us as a visitor"** signifies those who possess a different doctrine and a different life.
*   **And will he act as a judge?** <note>original: "judicabit judicando"</note> signifies: "Will they be the ones to teach us?"
*   **Now we will deal worse with you than with them** signifies that they would reject the good of charity even more than the Divine Human <note>original: "Divinum Humanum"</note> and the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Lord.
*   **And they pressed hard against the man** signifies that they wanted to do violence to the truth.
*   **Against Lot** signifies especially to the good of charity.
*   **And they came near to break down the door** signifies that they reached the point of attempting to destroy both truth and charity.

### Paragraph 2369
**"And they said"** signifies a response of anger, as is clear from the preceding and following context; thus, it requires no further explanation.

### Paragraph 2370
**"Stand back"** signifies threats of anger—specifically against the good of charity. This is clear from the symbolic meaning of Lot, who represents the good of charity, and to whom these words were addressed. That these are threats of anger is obvious from the words themselves and from what follows. It implies they would utterly reject that good if Lot spoke more about it or tried to persuade them. This is the meaning of "stand back."

### Paragraph 2371
**"And they said, 'This one man came to stay among us as a visitor'"** signifies those who have a different doctrine and a different life. This is clear from the meaning of "staying as a visitor" <note>original: "peregrinari"</note>, which means to be instructed and to live—referring to doctrine and life (as discussed in entries 1463 and 2025). 

Here, the state of the Church is described as it exists in its final times, when there is no longer any faith because there is no charity. In this state, the good of charity is rejected even from doctrine because it has entirely departed from people's lives. We are not talking here about those who falsify the good of charity by interpreting it in their own favor—doing so for their own status, or to possess the world’s wealth, or by claiming the power to distribute rewards, thus defiling charity with various tricks and deceptive methods. Instead, this refers to those who want to hear nothing of the goods of charity or good works, but only of "faith" separated from them—and this based on [reasoning]...

# CHAPTER NINETEEN

### Paragraph 2368 (continued)

By reasoning, some conclude that there is nothing but evil in man, and that any good coming from the man himself is also inherently evil, containing no salvation. They argue that because no one can merit <note>original: "mereri" – to earn or deserve a spiritual reward</note> heaven through any good deed, salvation comes not through works but solely through a faith by which people acknowledge the merit of the Lord. This is a doctrine that flourishes and is eagerly taught and accepted in the "latter times," when the Church begins to fade away. 

However, it is false to conclude from this that someone can lead a wicked life and yet possess a "good faith." This is false because since there is nothing but evil in a person, no good can exist unless it is given by the Lord. Because the Lord is present in that good, Heaven is there; and because Heaven is there, happiness and bliss are there. Furthermore, while it is true that no one can merit anything through their own good deeds, celestial good is still given by the Lord—a good in which the idea of personal "merit" is viewed as something distorted and monstrous. All angels live in this kind of good, as do all who are regenerated <note>original: "regenerati" – those undergoing a spiritual rebirth</note>, and those who perceive delight or even bliss in the act of doing good or in the affection for it.

Regarding this good, or this charity <note>original: "charitate"</note>, the Lord says in Matthew:

> "You have heard that it was said, 'You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.' But I say to you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who hurt and persecute you, so that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? and if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?" (Matthew 5:43–48)

Similarly, in Luke, with these additions:

> "Do good and lend, hoping for nothing in return; then your reward will be great, and you will be children of the Most High." (Luke 6:35)

Here is described the good that comes from the Lord, which is performed without any goal of being paid back. For this reason, those who live in this good are called "children of the Father in heaven" and "children of the Most High." And because the Lord is within that good, there is indeed a "reward," as described in Luke:

> "When you give a lunch or a supper, do not call your friends, or your brothers, or your relatives, or your rich neighbors, lest they perhaps invite you in return and you are repaid. But when you give a feast, invite the poor, the crippled, the blind; then you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you; for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the dead <note>original: "resurrectione mortuorum"</note>." (Luke 14:12–14)

A "lunch," "supper," or "feast" signifies the good of charity, in which the Lord dwells with man (see note 2341). For this reason, it is described this way, and it is clearly evident that the "repayment" exists within the good itself because the Lord is there; this is why it is said they will be "repaid at the resurrection of the dead."

Those who strive to do good of their own accord because the Lord commanded it are the ones who eventually receive this genuine good. Once they are instructed, they acknowledge by faith that all good is from the Lord (see notes 1712, 1937, 1947). At that point, they loathe the idea of their own "merit" so much that even thinking about it makes them sad, as they feel their sense of bliss and happiness diminish. 

It is different for those who do not live this way, but instead lead a life of evil while teaching and professing that salvation lies in "faith alone" <note>original: "fide separata" – faith separated from charity/works</note>. Such people do not even know that this kind of selfless good is possible. Surprisingly, in the next life—as has been shown through much experience—these same people try to claim heaven based on whatever "good" deeds they can remember. They do this because they only then realize that there is no salvation in a faith separated from charity. These are the people of whom the Lord says in Matthew:

> "Many will say to Me on that day, 'Lord, Lord, did we not [prophesy] in your Name...'" <note>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword "pheta-" indicates the next page begins with "prophetavimus" (prophesied).</note>

<summary>This page critiques the doctrine of "faith alone," arguing that true salvation involves selfless charity where the Lord is present. It explains that while humans cannot "earn" heaven, those who act out of genuine charity find their reward within the act itself because the Lord dwells there.</summary>

Among these same people, it also appears that they paid no attention at all to all those things that the Lord Himself so often taught concerning the good of love and charity. Instead, those teachings were like passing clouds or visions in the night. This is evident in passages such as: Matthew 3:8–9; Chapter 5:7–48; Chapter 6:1–20; Chapter 7:16–20 and 24–27; Chapter 9:13; Chapter 12:33; Chapter 13:8, 23; Chapter 18:21–23 to the end; Chapter 19:19; Chapter 22:34–39; Chapter 24:12–13; Chapter 25:34 to the end; Mark 4:18–20; Chapter 11:13, 14, 20; Chapter 12:28–35; Luke 3:8–9; Chapter 4:43–49; Chapter 6:27–39 and 43 to the end; Chapter 7:47; Chapter 8:8, 14, 15; Chapter 10:25–28; Chapter 12:58–59; Chapter 13:6–10; John 3:19, 21; Chapter 5:42; Chapter 13:34–35; Chapter 14:14, 15, 20, 21, 23; Chapter 15:1–8 and 9–19; Chapter 21:15, 16, 17.

**2372.** "**And he will act as a judge**," which signifies "will they teach us," is evident from the meaning of "judging," which is to teach. It has been shown (section 2235) that "Justice" is used when speaking of the practice of good, while "Judgment" <note>original: "Judicium"</note> is used when speaking of instruction in truth. Therefore, in the internal sense, "to judge" means to instruct or teach. To teach truth is the same as teaching what is good, because all truth looks toward what is good.

**2373.** "**Now we will treat you worse than them**" <note>original: "malefaciemus tibi præ illis"</note> signifies that they would reject the good of charity even more than they would reject the <term>Divine Human</term> <note>the Lord's divine nature in human form</note> and the Holy Proceeding of the Lord. This can be seen from the significance of Lot, who represents those who are in the good of charity (sections 2324, 2351, 2371). It also follows from the significance of the "men" or "angels" mentioned above, who represent the Lord regarding His Divine Human and the Holy Proceeding. 

The reason that those within the Church who are in evil reject charity more than they deny the Lord is that they can then indulge their own lusts through a form of religion. They can maintain an external worship without any internal worship—that is, worship with the mouth but not the heart. The more they make this worship appear "divine" and "holy," the more they gain in status and profit. There are many other hidden reasons, yet they are still visible: when someone rejects one of these (the doctrine and the life together), they also reject the other. Even if they do not dare to do so with their words, they still do so in their heart. This is expressed in the literal sense by the fact that they "stepped forward to break down the door." This signifies that they reached the point of attempting to destroy both charity and the Divine. What prevents this attempt from breaking out into actual deed is no secret.

**2374.** "**They pressed hard against the man**" signifies that they wanted to do violence to the truth. This is evident from the meaning of "man" <note>original: "virum"</note>, which refers to the intellectual and rational part of a person, and because this part is associated with truth (see sections 158, 1007). To do violence to the truth is to pervert... <note>The text continues on the next page; original Latin catchword: "pervertere"</note>
