...whether regarding truth. In this verse, where the **Divine Rational** <term>Divine Rational</term> <note>The highest level of the human mind, made Divine by the Lord.</note> or the **Divine Human** <term>Divine Human</term> <note>The glorified human nature of the Lord, which is both God and Man.</note> of the Lord is represented by Isaac <note>original: "Jischakum"</note>, the text uses a word for "possession by hereditary right." This is because the Lord’s Divine Human is the Sole Possessor and Heir, as He Himself teaches in the parable in Matthew 21:33, 37, 38; Mark 12:7; and Luke 20:14. He also declares in various places that all things belonging to the Father are His. 

When "to possess as an inheritance" and "to inherit" are used in the Word <note>original: "Verbo" — Swedenborg's term for the Bible.</note> in reference to people, it signifies receiving life from the Lord—and therefore eternal life or heaven—since only those who receive the Lord's life receive heaven. This is established in the book of Revelation: "He who overcomes *will inherit all things, and I will be his God, and he will be My son*" (Revelation 21:7) <note>original: "hæreditario accipiet omnia, & ero illi Deus, & ille erit Mihi filius"</note>. It is also seen in Matthew: "Everyone who has left houses, or brothers, or sisters... for My Name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold, *and will inherit eternal life*" (Matthew 19:29) <note>original: "& vitæ æternæ sortietur hæreditatem"</note>. See also Matthew 25:34; Mark 10:17; and Luke 18:18. In these passages, heaven is called "eternal life," and elsewhere simply "life" (as in Matthew 18:8–9, 19:17; John 3:36, 5:24, 29). This is because the Lord is Life itself, and whoever receives His life is in heaven. 

In the Psalms, it is written: "God will save Zion and build the cities of Judah, and they will dwell there and *possess it as an inheritance; and the offspring of His servants will inherit it*, and those who love His Name will dwell in it" (Psalm 69:36–37). Here, "possessing as an inheritance" refers to those who are in celestial love, while "inheriting" refers to those in spiritual love. 

Similarly, in Isaiah: "He who trusts in Me *will inherit the land, and will possess My holy mountain as an inheritance*" (Isaiah 57:13). 

And in the books of Moses: "I will bring you to the land... to give it to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and I will give it to you as a *possession of inheritance*" (Exodus 6:8). In the literal sense, these words mean that the land of Canaan would be given to them as an inheritance, which did happen. But in the **internal sense** <term>internal sense</term> <note>The deeper spiritual meaning of the Bible that lies beneath the literal stories.</note>, they signify that heaven would be given to those who are in love and faith toward the Lord. Just as the Lord is represented by Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, these figures also signify love itself and faith itself; therefore, they represent those who are in love and faith, and thus those who are in the Lord. 

This is also why it is said that many will sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the Kingdom of Heaven (Matthew 8:11). In heaven, the actual individuals Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are entirely unknown; the angels only know what is represented and signified by them, just as they know what "sitting down" or "eating" with them signifies. For the fact that all names in the Word signify actual spiritual realities, see sections 1224, 1264, 1876, and 1888. The "land of Canaan" refers to the "heavenly Canaan" or heaven (sections 1585, 1607, 1866), which is also simply called "the land" (sections 1413, 1607, 1733, 2571), as in Matthew: "Blessed are the poor <note>original: "miseri" — though usually translated as "meek" in the Beatitudes, the Latin here emphasizes the lowly or wretched state.</note>, for they will inherit the earth" (Matthew 5:5).

**"Because of his son"** signifies that He felt this way because He loved that Rational part.

2660. **This matter was very distressing in Abraham’s eyes** <note>original: "Malum fuit verbum valde in oculis Abrahami"</note>. This signifies the Lord’s first state when He considered separating that Rational part from Himself—specifically, that it was a state of grief stemming from love. This is evident without further explanation.

2661. **On account of his son** <note>original: "Ob causas filii sui"</note>. This signifies that He felt this way because He loved that first **Rational** <term>Rational</term> <note>The "Rational" refers to the level of the mind where human reasoning begins. Here, it refers to the Lord's initial, merely human reasoning before it was made Divine.</note>. This is clear from the meaning of "son" (referring here to the son of the Egyptian handmaid, Hagar), which represents the purely human or first Rational mind, as discussed previously. 

The cause of this grief is not explicitly stated here, but it is clear from what follows that it arises from love. The text says "his son," and the narrative discusses him from verse 13 to 21. To understand why this grief occurs—or why it is said that "this matter was very distressing in Abraham's eyes on account of his son"—the following points provide some light: 

The Lord did not come into the world to save the "celestial" <term>celestial</term> <note>Those who live primarily from a state of love and direct perception of God.</note>, but to save the "spiritual" <term>spiritual</term> <note>Those who live primarily from a state of faith and conscience, rather than direct love.</note>. The **Most Ancient Church** <note>Swedenborg’s term for the earliest state of humanity (represented by Adam), which was "celestial."</note>, which was called "Man," was celestial. If this church had remained in its integrity, there would have been no need for the Lord to be born as a man. Therefore, as soon as this church began to fail, the Lord foresaw that the celestial church would utterly vanish from the earth. Immediately, a prediction was made concerning the Lord's coming into the world (Genesis 3:15). 

After the time of that Church, there was no longer a celestial church, but a spiritual church. The **Ancient Church** <note>Represented by Noah.</note>, which existed after the flood, was a spiritual church. This church—or those who belong to the spiritual church—could not have been saved unless the Lord had come into the world. This is what is meant by the Lord's words in Matthew: **“**Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick; I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance**”** (Matthew 9:12–13). It is also meant by: **“**And I have other sheep which are not of this fold; I must bring them also, and they will hear My voice; and there will be one flock and one Shepherd**”** (John 10:16); and also by the parable of the hundred sheep in Matthew 18:11–13. 

Now, because Isaac represents the Lord’s **Divine Rational**, he also signifies the "celestial" who are called "heirs." Because Ishmael represents the Lord’s **merely human Rational**, he also signifies the "spiritual" who are called "sons," as is clear from what was said above (number 2658). Because of His Divine love, the Lord felt the grief expressed in this verse. This also explains the following section (verses 13 to 21), where Hagar's son and his mother represent the spiritual church and the state of those who belong to it. These secrets <note>original: "Arcana"</note> cannot be explained more fully yet; it is enough to know that while the Lord was in the world, all states of the Church were represented in Him, as well as how they would be saved through Him. Therefore, these same states of the Church are signified by the same names.

2662. Verse 12: *But God said to Abraham, "Do not be distressed about the boy and your slave woman. Listen to everything Sarah tells you, because it is through Isaac that your offspring will be reckoned."* 

**God said to Abraham** signifies the Lord’s perception from the Divine. 

**Do not be distressed about the boy and your slave woman** signifies a change of state.

2663. **God said to Abraham**. This signifies the Lord’s **perception** <term>perception</term> <note>An internal "sensing" or direct understanding from the Divine.</note> from the Divine. This is clear from the meaning of "to say" in the historical accounts of the **Word** <note>The Bible/Scripture</note>, which signifies "to perceive," as often mentioned before. Because this perception is from the Divine, it says "God said to Abraham." 

In both names—"God" and "Abraham"—the Lord is meant. While the historical narrative (the **literal sense** <term>literal sense</term>) divides ideas, the **internal sense** <term>internal sense</term> unites them. In the historical literal sense, there are two individuals—God and Abraham—who speak to each other. However, in the internal sense, there is only one: the Lord regarding His Divine nature. From this, it is also clear that those who appear as three in the literal sense are one in the internal sense—just as the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are not three gods, but one. In the Lord, every perfect **Trinity** <term>Trinity</term> <note>original: "Trinum"</note> exists: the Father is in Him (as He says), and the Holy Spirit proceeds from Him (as He also says).

2664. **Do not let it be evil in your eyes regarding the boy and your handmaid**. This signifies a change of state toward that **Rational** part. Furthermore, He did not grieve because it was a perception from the Divine that this separation was necessary; otherwise, the human race could not have been saved. This "change of state" is what is signified here.

2665. **Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice**. This signifies that He should act according to **spiritual truth**. This is clear from the representation of **Sarah**, who represents the **Divine Spiritual**, or **Divine Truth** (see n. 2622); and from the meaning of "listening to a voice," which means acting according to it (see n. 2542). 

What it means to "act according to spiritual truth" cannot be easily explained to the common understanding, though it can be perceived by those who are in the internal sense. Therefore, if the explanation were tailored only to their perception, it would hardly be recognized by others. This is because many **arcana** <term>arcana</term> <note>hidden spiritual secrets or mysteries</note> must first be unfolded—and indeed believed—before the explanation can enter one's thoughts of faith. In general, it means that the Lord reached a conclusion from His **Divine Human** and acted according to it—thus from His own power. For it was through **Divine Truth** that He united the Human to the Divine, and through **Divine Good** that He united the Divine to the Human (for more on this reciprocal union, see n. 2004).

2666. **In Isaac your seed shall be called**. This signifies that all salvation for those in **good** comes from the Lord’s **Divine Human**. This is clear from the representation of **Isaac** <note>original: "Jifchako"</note> as the **Divine Rational** (as stated before), and thus the **Divine Human**, for the human nature begins in the inmost part of the Rational (see n. 2106). It is also clear from the meaning of "seed" when applied to Isaac: it refers to the **celestial Rational**, or, what is the same, those who are "celestial" (see n. 2085, 2661). Thus, "to be called your seed" signifies that they are heirs, and consequently, that they have salvation. The "spiritual" are also "seed," but they come from the son of the handmaid, as mentioned in the following verse: "And also No. VI. the son..."

They are like unripe fruit, which cannot be given its shape, beauty, and flavor in a single moment; or like tender shoots that cannot grow into a flower or an ear of grain instantly. This is done for his benefit as much as is possible, provided the person allows himself to be led by the Lord.

...to be in poverty and hunger, solitary, to flee to dryness, past night, desolation, and vastness; to live in the fissures of valleys and rocks, then to pluck mallows from the bush, and groan among the shrubs. As it also says in Isaiah: "They will come and all rest in the rivers of *desolations* <note>original: "defolationum"</note>, in the fissures of the rocks, and in all the shrubs, and in all the conduits" (Isaiah 7:19). This verse deals with the second state of those who are being **reformed** <term>reformed</term> <note>The process of being led by the Lord from a natural, worldly state toward a spiritual one.</note>. This state is when they are reduced to a level of ignorance where they know nothing of truth, leading them even to despair. The reason they are reduced to such ignorance is to extinguish the **persuasive light** <term>persuasive light</term> <note>original: "lux persuasiva"; a type of intellectual self-confidence where a person convinces themselves that something is true based on their own ego or desires, rather than genuine spiritual insight.</note>. This light is of such a nature that it illuminates both falsehoods and truths equally; it leads a person to believe in what is false by using truths, and to believe in what is true by using falsehoods, all while building up self-confidence. 

Furthermore, they are led into this state so that they may learn through actual experience that nothing of "good" or "truth" comes from themselves or from their **own power** <term>own power</term> <note>original: "proprio"; the sense of self or the ego that believes it is the source of its own life and wisdom.</note>, but only from the Lord. Those being reformed are brought into ignorance to the point of despair, and only then do they receive comfort and enlightenment, as is clear from what follows. The light of truth from the Lord cannot flow into a persuasive state that originates from the self; that self-centered state is such that it actually extinguishes the Lord's light. In the afterlife, this "persuasive light" looks like the cold light of winter; but as it approaches the light of heaven, it becomes dark, and in that darkness exists an utter ignorance of truth. 

This state is called the "desolation of truth" in those being reformed, and it is discussed extensively in the **internal sense of the Word** <term>internal sense of the Word</term> <note>The deeper, spiritual meaning of the Bible that lies beneath the literal stories.</note>. However, few people today can understand this state because few are being **regenerated** <term>regenerated</term> <note>The process of spiritual rebirth.</note>. To those who are not being regenerated, it doesn't matter whether they know the truth or not, or even if what they know is actually true, as long as they can pretend something is true for their own benefit. But those who are being regenerated think deeply about doctrine and life because they care about eternal salvation. Therefore, if they find they lack truth—since truth is the focus of their thought and affection—they grieve in their hearts. 

The difference between these two types of people can be seen in this: while a person is in the body, their spirit lives in heaven and their body lives in the world. We are born into both. A person is created so that their spirit can actually be with angels while their body is with humans. But because so few people believe they have a spirit that lives after death, few are being regenerated. For those who do believe, the afterlife is the focus of all their thought and affection, and the world is nothing by comparison. But for those who do not believe, the world is everything, and the afterlife is nothing. The former are those who can be regenerated; the latter are those who cannot.

### Verse 16. *And she went, and sat her down over against him, a good way off, as it were a bowshot; for she said, Let me not see the death of the child. And she sat over against him, and lifted up her voice, and wept.*

2683. **"She went, and sat her down over against him"** signifies a state of thought. **"A good way off, as it were a bowshot"** signifies the state of how far they were from the **doctrine of truth**; for a "bow" <term>bow</term> <note>In spiritual symbolism, a bow represents doctrine, as it is the tool that "fires" truths (arrows).</note> is the doctrine of truth. **"Because she said, Let me not see the death of the child"** signifies the grief that truth would perish in this way. **"And she sat over against him"** signifies a state of thought. **"And she lifted up her voice and wept"** signifies a further degree of grief.

### CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE

Regarding the events that come before and after: to go—or in this case, to go away from the boy—signifies a removal from spiritual truth. This is further described and defined by the fact that she distanced herself "about a bowshot’s distance." Sitting by herself signifies a solitary state, such as that of a mind in pain and despair. The phrase "opposite" <note>original: "e regione"</note> signifies that she would not look upon him, yet she continued to watch; for "to look" means to think (as seen in section 2245). This is further defined by her saying, "Let me not see the death of the boy," as she sat opposite him. Thus, these words represent the state of thought of those who are in a desolation of truth and the resulting despair.

2685. **Distancing herself about a bowshot’s distance**, which signifies a state of how far one is from the **doctrine of truth** <term>doctrine of truth</term> <note>The systematic body of teachings or principles derived from the Word of God.</note>. This is evident from the meaning of "distancing," which is to be absent, and from the meaning of a "bow," which is the doctrine of truth (discussed below). A "shot" signifies being as far away as possible, just as a dart is shot from a bow as far as it can go. Here, a "bowshot" is mentioned because the "bow" is associated with the spiritual person, who is called an "archer" <note>original: "jaculator arcus"</note> in the following verse 20: "And he lived in the wilderness, and was an archer."

2686. That a **bow** represents the doctrine of truth is evident from its meaning. In the Word, wherever "Wars" are discussed and mentioned, in the **internal sense** <term>internal sense</term> <note>The deeper, spiritual meaning of the Bible that lies beneath the literal stories and historical accounts.</note>, no other wars are meant than spiritual ones (section 1664). There were even books in the Ancient Church titled *The Wars of Jehovah*, as is clear in Moses (Numbers 21:14–16). These were written in a prophetic style and contained an internal sense, dealing with the Lord's battles and temptations, as well as those of the Church and its members. This is evident because Moses took excerpts from them, as well as from other books of that Church called *The Books of Prophetic Sayings* <note>original: "Libri Enuntiatorum propheticorum"</note> (Numbers 21:27–30). In these, the words are almost identical to those found in Jeremiah (compare Numbers 21:28 and Jeremiah 48:45). From this, it can be concluded that the Ancient Church had both historical and prophetic writings that were Divine and inspired, which in their internal sense dealt with the Lord and His Kingdom. These were their "Word," just as the historical and prophetic books are for us; while our books deal with the Jews and Israelites in the literal sense, in the internal sense they deal with the Lord and the things belonging to Him.

Because "War" in the Word (as well as in the books of the Ancient Church) signified spiritual war, all weapons—such as the sword, spear, shield, buckler, darts, arrows, and the bow—signified specific things belonging to war understood in a spiritual sense. What each specific weapon signifies will, by the Lord's Divine Mercy, be discussed elsewhere. For now, we address the **Bow**: it signifies the doctrine of truth. This is derived from the "darts," "arrows," or "weapons," which are the doctrinal principles from which and with which people fight—especially those who are spiritual, who were therefore anciently called "Archers" <note>original: "Jaculatores arcus"</note>. That a bow signifies the doctrine of truth can be seen from these passages; in Isaiah: "Jehovah's arrows are sharp, and all His bows are bent; His horses' hooves are regarded like rock, and His wheels like a whirlwind" (Isaiah 5:28). Here, the subject is the truths of doctrine: the arrows are spiritual truths, the **bow** is doctrine, the horses' hooves are natural things, and the wheels are their teachings. Because these things have such meanings, they are attributed to Jehovah—to whom they could only be attributed in a spiritual sense; otherwise, the words would be meaningless.

In the book of Habakkuk: "O Jehovah, you rode upon your horses; your chariots were salvation. Your **bow** <note>original: "Arcus tuus"</note> was stripped completely bare" (Habakkuk 3:8, 9). There, the bow also represents the doctrine of good and truth.

In the writings of Moses: "The **archers** <note>original: "sagittarii"</note> will provoke him, and shoot at him, and hate him; but his **bow** <note>original: "Arcus sui"</note> will remain in strength, and the arms of his hands will be made strong by the hands of the mighty Jacob; from there is the Shepherd, the Stone of Israel" (Genesis 49:23, 24). In the book of John: "I looked, and behold, a white horse; and he who sat upon it had a **bow** <note>original: "Arcum"</note>, and a crown was given to him" (Revelation 6:2). Because the one sitting upon it is the Word, it is certain that the bow represents the doctrine of truth.

In the book of Isaiah: "Who raised up righteousness from the east, called him to follow him, gave the nations before him, and made him rule over kings? He gave them like dust to his sword, and like driven stubble to his **bow**" (Isaiah 41:2). This passage concerns the Lord; the sword represents truth, and the bow represents the doctrine that comes from Him.

"Drawing the bow" <note>original: "trahentes arcum"</note> signifies teaching doctrine. (For what Tarshish signifies, see section 1156; for Lud, see sections 1195, 1231; for Tubal, see section 1151; and for Javan, see sections 1152, 1153, 1155).

In the book of Jeremiah: "At the noise of the horseman and the **bowman** <note>original: "jacientis arcum"</note>, the whole city flees; they entered the clouds and climbed the rocks; the whole city is deserted" (Jeremiah 4:29). The horseman represents those who speak the truth, while the bow represents the doctrine of truth, which those who dwell in falsehoods flee from or fear.

In the same book: "Set the battle lines against Babylon all around, all you who **bend the bow**; shoot at her, do not spare the arrows, for she has sinned against Jehovah" (Jeremiah 50:14, 29; Chapter 51:2, 3). Here, those who "shoot" and "bend the bow" represent those who speak and teach the doctrine of truth.

In the book of Zechariah: "I will cut off the **chariot** from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and the **bow of war** <note>original: "arcus belli"</note> will be cut off, and he will speak peace to the nations" (Zechariah 9:10). Ephraim represents the understanding of the Church's truth, and the bow represents doctrine.

In the book of Samuel: "David lamented this lamentation over Saul and over Jonathan his son, and he told them to teach the children of Judah the **bow**" (2 Samuel 1:17). This does not actually concern a physical bow, but rather the **doctrines of faith** <term>doctrines of faith</term> <note>The formal spiritual teachings that define a religious belief system.</note>.

In the book of Ezekiel: "The word of the Lord Jehovah: This is the day of which I have spoken; and the inhabitants of the cities of Israel will go out and set on fire and burn the weapons—the shield and the buckler, the **bow** and the arrows, the handstaff and the spear—and they will burn them with fire for seven years" (Ezekiel 39:9). The weapons named here are all weapons of spiritual war; the bow and its arrows represent doctrine and its specific truths. Indeed, in the afterlife, when truths separated from goodness are represented visually, they actually appear as arrows. Just as a bow signifies the doctrine of truth, in the opposite sense, it also signifies the doctrine of falsehood; similar patterns occur throughout the Word...

**2689.** The phrase **and she lifted up her voice and wept** signifies a further degree of grief. This is evident from the meaning of "lifting up one's voice and weeping," which represents the ultimate expression of sorrow; for weeping with a loud voice is nothing else. This verse describes a state of "desolation of truth" and a sense of being distanced from truths among those who are becoming spiritual.

They think it is impossible for anyone to be distressed by such a thing. They believe the only possible anxiety is when someone is deprived of worldly or physical goods—such as health, honor, reputation, wealth, or life itself. However, those who *can* be reformed...

# GENESIS

Others believe quite differently; they are held by the Lord in an **affection for good** <note>original: *affectione boni*</note> and in a **thought of truth** <note>original: *cogitatione veri*</note>. For this reason, they fall into anxiety when they are deprived of these things. It is well known that all anxiety and pain arise from being deprived of those things with which one is affected, or those things which one loves. Those who are only affected by bodily and worldly things, or who love only such things, grieve when they lose them. However, those who are affected by spiritual goods and truths, and love them, grieve when they are deprived of them. 

The life of every person is nothing other than **affection** <term>affectio—the state of being moved by a particular love or desire</term> or love. From this, it can be established what the state is of those who are "desolated" regarding the goods and truths with which they are affected or which they love. Their state of grief is more severe because it is more internal; in the deprivation of good and truth, they do not look toward the death of the body (which they do not care about), but toward eternal death. It is their state that is described here. 

To understand who can be held by the Lord in the affection for good and truth—and thus be reformed and become spiritual—and who cannot, a few things must be said. Everyone in childhood, when first being imbued with goods and truths, is held by the Lord in an **affirmative state** <note>original: *affirmativo*</note>: the belief that what is said and taught by parents and teachers is true. 

In those who are capable of becoming spiritual, this affirmative state is confirmed through scientific facts and knowledge. Whatever they learn that is related to it insinuates itself into this affirmative state and strengthens it, doing so more and more until it becomes an affection. These are the people who become "spiritual" according to the essence of the truth in which they have faith, and who are victorious in spiritual **temptations** <term>tentationes—inner struggles between good and evil or truth and falsehood</term>. 

However, it is quite different for those who cannot become spiritual. Even though they are in an affirmative state during childhood, as they grow older, they allow **doubts** <note>original: *dubitativa*</note> to enter, and thus they break down the affirmative state of good and truth. When they enter adulthood, they admit **negatives** <note>original: *negativa*</note>, eventually leading to an affection for what is false. If these people were led into spiritual trials, they would completely fail; for this reason, they are spared from them. 

The primary cause for admitting doubts and later negatives stems entirely from a **life of evil** <note>original: *vita mali*</note>. Those who live an evil life can never do otherwise. As stated, the life of every person is their affection or love; as the affection is, so is the thought. An affection for evil and a thought of truth never truly join together. Where they appear to join, they still do not truly unite; it is merely a thought of truth without an affection for it. Therefore, in such people, truth is not really truth, but only a kind of sound or speech from the mouth, from which the heart is far away. Even the worst people can know such truth, sometimes even better than others. 

In some people, there is even a "persuasive" belief in truth of such a nature that no one could tell it is anything but genuine; yet it is not genuine if there is no **life of good** <note>original: *vita boni*</note>. It is the affection of self-love or love of the world that induces such a persuasive belief, which they defend with the intensity of apparent zeal—even to the point of condemning those who do not receive it or believe in the same way. But this "truth" is only a starting principle for them, and it is stronger the stronger their self-love or love of the world is. It is indeed attached to evil, but it does not join with evil; therefore, it is uprooted in the next life. 

It is different for those who are in a life of good: there, truth itself has its soil, its heart, and its life from the Lord.

# CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE

> *[God called to] Hagar from heaven and said to her, "What is the matter, Hagar? Do not fear, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is."* <note>original: "Hagarem e cælo, & dixit ei, quid tibi Hagar, ne timeas, quia audivit Deus vocem pueri, in quo ille est."</note> "God heard the voice of the boy" signifies that help was given at that time. "The angel of God called to Hagar from heaven" signifies consolation. "And said to her, 'What is the matter, Hagar?'" signifies a perception of her state. "Do not fear, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is" signifies the hope of help.

**2691.** **God heard the voice of the boy** signifies help at that time. This is evident from the meaning of "God hearing a voice" in the literal history, which in the **internal sense** <term>internal sense—the deeper, spiritual meaning of the Bible hidden beneath the literal words</term> means to bring help. It is also evident from the meaning of "the boy," which signifies **spiritual truth** <note>original: *spirituale verum*</note>, as discussed previously. In this context, it refers to the state in which the spiritual person is regarding truth; for the text says "He heard the voice of the boy *where he is*" (that is, in whatever state he is in), and the preceding verses described him being in a state of extreme grief due to a lack of truth.

The reason the text says God heard the "voice of the boy" rather than the voice of Hagar is that the subject here is the state of the spiritual person. The "boy" (Ishmael) represents the person of the **Spiritual Church** <term>Spiritual Church—a state of faith and charity where truth is the primary guide to life</term>. Hagar, his mother, represents the **affection for the knowledge of truth** <note>original: *affectio cognitionum veri*</note>, which is the part of the person experiencing the grief. A person's **rationality** <note>original: *Rationale*</note> is born from an affection for sciences as if from a mother (see numbers 1895, 1896, 1902, 1910, 2094, 2524); but their **spiritual nature** <note>original: *Spirituale*</note> is born from an affection for the knowledge of truth derived from doctrine, and especially from the Word of God. This spiritual nature is what the "boy" represents here, while the affection for that knowledge is represented by Hagar.

**2692.** **And the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven** signifies consolation. This is clear from the meaning of "calling from heaven," as well as the roles of the "angel of God" and "Hagar." "To call from heaven" signifies **influx** <term>influx—the flow of spiritual life or influence from God into a person's mind and heart</term>. The "angel of God" refers to the Lord (see numbers 1925, 2321), and "Hagar" signifies the affection for the knowledge of truth (number 2691). The Lord's influence into a person’s affection for truth, especially when that affection is in deep grief due to a lack of truth, results in **consolation**. What flows from the Lord into a person is described as being "called from heaven" because it passes through heaven and is clearly known there, though in a person’s own perception and thought it is obscure—only making itself known through a change in the state of their feelings, such as the consolation received here.

**2693.** **He said to her, "What is the matter, Hagar?"** signifies a perception of her state. This is evident from the meaning of "saying" in the historical accounts of the Word, which signifies **perceiving** (as discussed before), and from the phrase "What is the matter, Hagar?" which refers to the state she was in. Here it signifies that the Lord knew her state, even though she is asked the question. In the literal sense, it is a question from the Lord, but in the internal sense, it represents the Lord's infinite perception of everything. The fact that people are often asked about their state in the Word is because a person does not easily believe that anyone else knows their thoughts—much less the state of their feelings. It is also done so that they may find comfort by opening up the feelings of their mind, which often serves as a remedy (see numbers 1701, 1931).

**2694.** **"Do not fear, for God has heard the voice of the boy where he is"** signifies the hope of help. This is evident from the meaning of "do not fear," which means not to despair, for when fear is removed, hope arrives. It is also evident from "hearing the voice of the boy," which signifies help (as noted above in number 2691, where similar words appear). The preceding verses dealt with the state of **desolation** <term>desolation—a spiritual state of feeling abandoned or lacking the truth and goodness needed for spiritual life</term> experienced by those who are being **reformed** <term>reformed—the process of being spiritually changed and improved by the Lord</term>.

<header>GENESIS</header>

...are formed and become spiritual; now we are dealing with their restoration—specifically, with consolation and the hope of help. 

It is currently unknown that those being reformed are reduced to an ignorance of truth (or "desolation"), leading even to pain and despair, and that only then do they first receive consolation and help from the Lord. This is because few people today are truly reformed. Those who are capable of being reformed, if they do not experience this in their physical life, are brought into this state in the next life. This state is very well known there and is called **Vastation** or **Desolation** <term>Vastation—a process of spiritual "emptying" where a person's self-centered beliefs and illusions are cleared away to make room for divine truth</term> (see section 1109 in Part One). 

Those in such a state of vastation or desolation are brought to the point of despair. When they reach this state, they then receive comfort and help from the Lord. Eventually, they are taken from there into heaven, where they are instructed by angels, as if anew, in the "goods and truths" <note>the fundamental components of a spiritual life: good actions/intentions and true beliefs</note> of faith. 

The main reason for this vastation and desolation is to break the **persuasive power** <note>original: *persuasivum*</note> of the ideas they have formed from their own **selfhood** <term>selfhood—(Latin: *proprium*) the natural human tendency to believe that one's life, wisdom, and goodness originate in oneself rather than from God</term> (see section 2682). Another reason is so that they may gain a genuine perception of what is good and true. They cannot receive this perception until the self-willed persuasion has been softened. A state of anxiety and pain, leading even to despair, achieves this. 

No one can truly perceive what is good—or what is blessed and happy—unless they have first been in a state that is not good, not blessed, and not happy. From this contrast, the mind gains a "sphere of perception." The depth and extent of one's perception are actually formed by the degree of the opposite state they experienced. These are the reasons for vastation or desolation, among many others. 

Let us use examples for illustration. Consider those who attribute everything to their own prudence and little or nothing to **Divine Providence**. Even if they were shown a thousand reasons why Divine Providence is universal—and universal precisely because it is in the most minute details, such that not even a hair falls from the head (meaning not even the smallest thing happens) without being foreseen and provided for—their way of thinking about their own prudence would still not change. It might change for a single moment when they realize they are overwhelmed by logic; even if this were proven to them through **living experiences** <note>original: *vivas experientias*</note>, they would admit it while witnessing or undergoing the experience, but a few moments later they would return to their original opinion. 

Such things have only a temporary effect on the *thought*, but not on the **affection** <term>affection—the underlying desire or love that drives a person’s will and life</term>. Unless the affection is broken, the thought remains in its original state, for thought draws its faith and its life from affection. However, when they are led into anxiety and pain because they realize they can do nothing at all by themselves, and this is pushed to the point of despair, then their self-conviction is broken and their state is changed. Only then can they be led into the faith that they have no power of their own, but that all power, prudence, intelligence, and wisdom come from the Lord. 

The same applies to those who believe that faith or goodness originates from themselves. To provide a further example: take those who have convinced themselves that once they are **justified** <term>justified—in this context, the belief that one has been made righteous or "saved" from sin</term>, they no longer have any evil within them, but that it has been completely wiped away and deleted, leaving them pure. Even if they were shown a thousand reasons why nothing is actually "wiped away" or deleted, but rather that those who have lived a good life are held back from evil and kept in good by the Lord; and even if they were convinced by experiences...

2695. Verse 18. *Arise, lift up the lad, and strengthen your hand in him, for I will make him a great nation.*
**"Arise"** signifies the elevation of the mind. **"Lift up the lad"** signifies the spiritual aspect regarding truth. **"Strengthen your hand in him"** signifies the support derived from that truth. **"For I will make him a great nation"** signifies the spiritual Church.

2696. **"Arise"** signifies the elevation of the mind. This is clear from the meaning of "arising" in the Word <note>original: *in Verbo*—referring to the Bible</note>, which implies an elevation whenever it is mentioned (as seen in section 2401). Here, it refers to an elevation of the mind because it involves enlightenment and, in the following verse, instruction in truths.

2697. **"Lift up the lad"** signifies the spiritual aspect regarding truth. This is clear from the meaning of "the lad" <note>original: *puer*</note>, which specifically refers to the spiritual aspect regarding truth (as seen in sections 2677 and 2687). The person in the spiritual Church appears to be **regenerated** <term>regenerated—the process of being spiritually reborn or transformed by God</term> through the truths of faith. However, they are unaware that this happens through the **good of truth** <note>the inner motivation or "heart" that makes a person love and act upon what is true</note>. This "good" does not show itself directly; it only reveals itself in an affection for truth and later in a life lived according to truth. No one can ever be regenerated by truth alone, unless there is "good" within that truth. Truth without good has no life. Therefore, no new life—which a person receives through regeneration—can come from truth separated from good.

2698. **"Strengthen your hand in him"** signifies the support derived from that truth. This is clear from the meaning of "strengthening," which means to be supported, and "hand," which signifies power (as seen in section 878) and thus the power of support. "In him" (the lad) means from that source—namely, from the spiritual aspect of truth. Those who are in inner pain and despair because they feel deprived of truth are elevated and supported solely by truth, because truth is exactly what they feel the loss of. For those who feel an "affection for good," the good within them longs for more good, just as a hungry person craves bread. However, for those in an "affection for truth," the good within them longs for truth, just as a thirsty person craves water. The meaning of "strengthening the hand in him" cannot be understood by anyone except through the **internal sense** <term>internal sense—the deeper, spiritual meaning of the Bible that lies beneath the literal stories</term>.

2699. **"For I will make him a great nation"** signifies the spiritual Church. This is clear from the meaning of a "great nation" as the spiritual Church that is destined to receive the "good of faith" (as mentioned above in section 2669). It is called a "great nation"...

It is so stated because the Spiritual Kingdom is the other Kingdom of the Lord <note>original: *quia Regnum Spirituale est alterum Regnum Domini*</note>. As mentioned in the previous section, through Ishmael, just as the spiritual person of the Church is represented, so too is the spiritual Church itself represented, as well as the Lord's Spiritual Kingdom in the heavens; for the image and likeness of one is found in the other. 

The first state after **desolation** <term>desolation—a spiritual state of feeling abandoned or emptied of truth</term> was described in the preceding verse as a state of comfort and the hope of help. A second state after desolation is described in this verse: a state of **enlightenment** <term>original: *illustrationis*—a divine shedding of light upon the mind</term> and the subsequent refreshment it brings. 

Because these states are unknown in the world—since few today, as previously stated, are **regenerated** <term>regenerated—the process of being spiritually reborn or made new by the Lord</term>—it is helpful to describe what this state is like in the afterlife, where it is very well known. There, those who have been in "vastation" or desolation, after being comforted by the hope of help, are raised by the Lord into heaven. They are moved from a state of shadow (which is a state of ignorance) into a state of light (which is a state of enlightenment and the refreshment that follows), and thus into a joy that affects their innermost being. 

The light they enter is actual light, which is of such a nature that it illuminates not only their sight but also their intellect. How much this light refreshes them can be seen by comparing it to the opposite state from which they were delivered. At that time, those who possessed a childlike mind and a simple faith appear to themselves in white and shining garments; some appear in crowns. Some are carried around to many angelic societies and are everywhere received with love as brothers. There, whatever good from their new life is pleasing to them is presented. Some are permitted to see the immensity of heaven—the Lord’s Kingdom—and at the same time to perceive the happiness of those who live there, along with innumerable other things that cannot be described. Such is the state of the first enlightenment and the resulting refreshment for those who come out of spiritual desolation.

### 2700. Verse 19
**"And God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water, and she went and filled the skin with water and gave the lad a drink."**

**"God opened her eyes"** signifies intelligence. **"And she saw a well of water"** signifies the Word of the Lord <note>the Bible</note> from which truths come. **"And she filled the skin with water"** signifies the truths derived from it. **"And she gave the lad a drink"** signifies instruction in spiritual matters.

### 2701.
**"God opened her eyes"** signifies intelligence. This is evident from the meaning of "opening" (and that it is *God* opening) and from the "eyes," which signify the granting of intelligence. That "eyes" signify the intellect can be seen in section 212, as well as "sight" or "seeing" in sections 2150 and 2325. 

It is said that God "opens the eyes" when He opens the internal sight or intellect. This occurs through an **influx** <term>influx—the flow of divine life and light into the human mind</term> into the rational part of a person, or rather, into the spiritual part of their rational mind. This happens through the soul or the internal path, which is unknown to the person. This influx is the person's state of enlightenment, in which truths they hear or read are confirmed to them by a certain internal perception in their intellect. 

A person often believes this intelligence is inherent to them and comes from their own intellectual ability, but they are greatly mistaken. It is actually an influx through heaven from the Lord into the person's obscure, deceptive, and appearance-based nature. Through the "good" stored within them, the Lord makes those things they believe seem like truth. However, only those who are "spiritual" are blessed with this enlightenment regarding the spiritual matters of faith. This is what is signified by "God opening the eyes." The eye signifies the intellect because the physical sight of the body corresponds to the sight of the spirit, which is the intellect.

...chosen; and because it corresponds, the **eye** in the Word <note>original: *Verbo*—referring to the Holy Scriptures</note> signifies the **intellect** <term>intellect—the faculty of understanding and reasoning</term> almost everywhere it is named, even where it is believed to mean something else. This is seen where the Lord says in Matthew: "The lamp of the body is the eye; if your eye is simple <note>original: *simplex*—meaning clear or single-minded</note>, your whole body will be full of light; but if your eye is evil, your whole body will be full of darkness. If therefore the light that is in you is darkness, how great is that darkness!" (Matthew 6:22–23; Luke 11:34). In this passage, the "eye" is the intellect, and its spiritual quality is **faith**. This is also evident from the explanation given there: "If therefore the light is darkness, how great is that darkness." 

Similarly, the Lord says: "If your right eye causes you to sin, pluck it out and cast it from you" (Matthew 5:29, 18:9). The "left eye" represents the intellectual faculty, while the "right eye" represents its **affection** <term>affection—the emotional drive or love behind a thought</term>. The instruction to pluck out the right eye means that one's affection must be subdued if it leads one astray. 

Again, in Matthew: "Blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear" (Matthew 13:16); and in Luke: "Jesus said to his disciples, 'Blessed are the eyes that see what you see'" (Luke 10:23). Here, "eyes that see" signifies intelligence and faith. Simply seeing the Lord or His miracles and works did not make anyone blessed; rather, they were blessed because they grasped these things with their intellect and had faith—which is what "seeing with the eyes" means—and because they obeyed—which is what "hearing with the ears" means. To see with the eyes is to understand and to have faith (see also section numbers 897 and 2325). 

The intellect is effectively the "spiritual sight," and faith is the "spiritual intellect." The sight of the physical eye comes from the light of the natural world, while the sight of the intellect comes from the light of heaven flowing into the things of the natural world's light. Furthermore, the sight of faith comes directly from the light of heaven. This is why we speak of "seeing with the intellect" and "seeing by faith." To hear with the ear is to obey (see section 2542). 

In Mark, we read: "Jesus said to his disciples, 'Do you not yet perceive or understand? Is your heart still hardened? Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear?'" (Mark 8:17–18). Here it is clear that refusing to understand and refusing to believe is described as "having eyes but not seeing." In Luke, Jesus says of the city: "If you had known... what belongs to your peace! But now they are hidden from your eyes" (Luke 19:41–42). And in Mark: "This was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes" (Mark 12:11). That "hidden from the eyes" and "marvelous in the eyes" refers to the intellect is well known to everyone from the common use of the word "eye" even in everyday speech.

2702. **And she saw a well of water**, which signifies the Word of the Lord, from which truths come. This is clear from the symbolism of a "well of water" or a "fountain," which represents the Word, as well as the doctrine derived from the Word, and consequently Truth itself (as follows shortly). It is also clear from the symbolism of **water**, which represents truth. 

That a "well" containing water, or a "fountain," represents the Word of the Lord and the teaching drawn from it can be seen from many passages. Because this section deals with the **Spiritual Church** <note>original: *Ecclesia Spiritualis*</note>, the text uses the term "well" rather than "fountain." This is also seen later in this chapter: "Abraham rebuked Abimelech because of a well which Abimelech’s servants had seized" (Verse 25). Also in Genesis Chapter 26: "The Philistines had stopped up all the wells which his father Abraham’s servants had dug in the days of his father Abraham. And Isaac returned and dug the wells of water which they had dug in the days of Abraham his father, for the Philistines had stopped them up after..."

...the death of Abraham. "And Isaac's <note>original: *Jiſchaki*—the Latin form of the Hebrew name for Isaac</note> servants dug in the valley and found there a **well of living waters**. In this passage, **wells** signify nothing other than **doctrines** <note>original: *doctrinalia*—matters pertaining to religious teaching</note>, concerning which they either quarreled or did not quarrel. Otherwise, the fact that they dug wells and argued over them so many times would not be significant enough to be recorded in the Divine Word. 

Similarly, a **well** signifies the Word or doctrine, as mentioned in Moses: "They went to *Beer* <note>original: *Beer*—the Hebrew word for 'well'</note>; this is the *well* of which Jehovah said to Moses, 'Gather the people together, and I will give them *waters*.' The princes dug the *well*; the volunteers of the people dug it out, with the Lawgiver, with their staffs'" (Numbers <term>xxi</term>: 16, 17, 18). Because the well signified these things, this prophetic song of Israel deals with the **doctrine of truth**, as is clear from every detail in its internal sense. From this comes the name *Beer*, and the name *Beer-sheba*, and its meaning in the internal sense: that it is doctrine itself. 

However, a doctrine that does not contain truths is called a **pit** <term>pit—in Latin, *fovea*, often referring to a dry or broken cistern</term>, or a well in which there is no water. As seen in Jeremiah: "Their nobles sent their children <note>original: *minores*—literally 'lesser ones' or 'little ones'</note> for *water*; they came to the *pits* and found no *water*; they returned with their vessels empty" (Jeremiah <term>xiv</term>: 3). Here, "waters" represent truths, and the "pits" where they found no water represent doctrine in which there is no truth. In the same prophet: "My people have committed two evils: they have forsaken Me, the **spring of living waters**, to dig for themselves pits—broken pits that cannot hold *water*" (Jeremiah <term>ii</term>: 13). Here, likewise, "pits" represent doctrines that are not true, and "broken pits" represent compiled doctrines that are faulty.

A **fountain** <note>original: *fons*—a natural spring or source</note> represents the Word, as well as doctrine, and therefore truth itself. In Isaiah: "The afflicted and needy seeking waters, and there are none; their tongue fails for thirst. I, Jehovah, will hear them; the God of Israel will not forsake them. I will open rivers on the hills and fountains in the midst of the valleys; I will make the desert a pool of water, and the dry land into *springs of water*" (Isaiah <term>xli</term>: 17, 18). This refers to the "desolation of truth," signified by the afflicted seeking water in vain and their tongues failing from thirst. It then describes the consolation, restoration, and instruction after that desolation (as in the verses concerning Hagar). These are signified by Jehovah opening rivers on the hills, placing fountains in the valleys, and turning the desert into a pool of water and the dry land into springs—all of which represent the doctrines of truth and the affection <term>affection—the spiritual love or desire for truth</term> that flows from them. 

In Moses: "Israel dwelt safely alone at the *fountain of Jacob*, in a land of grain and new wine; even his heavens drop down dew" (Deuteronomy <term>xxxiii</term>: 28). The "fountain of Jacob" represents the Word and the doctrine of truth derived from it. Because the fountain of Jacob signified the Word and the doctrine of truth, when the Lord came to the fountain of Jacob, He spoke with the woman from Samaria and taught what is signified by a fountain and by water. A woman from Samaria came to draw..." <note>original: *haurien-*—the text cuts off at the start of 'drawing'</note>

In Jeremiah: "Behold, I am bringing them from the north country, and will gather them from the farthest parts of the earth, among them the blind and the lame; they shall come with weeping, and with prayers I will lead them to fountains of waters in a straight way, and they shall not stumble in it" (Jeremiah 31:8–9). "Fountains of waters in a straight way" clearly stands for the doctrines of truth. The "north country" represents ignorance or the desolation of truth; "weeping and prayers" represent their state of grief and despair. To be led to "fountains of waters" represents refreshment and instruction in truths, just as in the story of Hagar and her son.

The same theme is found in Isaiah: "The desert and the dry land shall rejoice for them, and the wilderness shall exult and bloom like the rose; budding it shall bud, and exult even with exultation and singing; the glory of Lebanon is given to it, the honor of Carmel and Sharon; they shall see the glory of Jehovah, the honor of our God. Strengthen the weary hands and confirm the stumbling knees; the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped; waters shall break out in the desert, and rivers in the wilderness, and the parched ground shall become a pool, and the thirsty land springs of water" (Isaiah 35:1–3, 5–7). In this context, the "desert" represents the desolation of truth. Waters, rivers, pools, and springs of water represent the Truths that bring refreshment and joy to those who have been in a state of spiritual devastation <term>vastation—a state of being emptied of old ideas to make room for new truths</term>. Their joy is described here in many ways.

In David, "Jehovah sends out springs in the valleys; they flow between the mountains. Here, "springs" stand for truths; "mountains" stand for the love of good and truth; "to give drink" stands for to instruct; "wild beasts of the fields" stand for those who live from these truths (see numbers 774, 841, 908); and "wild donkeys" stand for those who are only in rational truth (numbers 1949, 1950, 1951).

In Moses, "Joseph is the son of a fruitful tree, the son of a fruitful tree by a spring" (Genesis 49:22). A "spring" <note>original: *fons*</note> stands for doctrine from the Lord. In the same author, "The land of Canaan is a land of mountains and valleys; it drinks waters from the rain of heaven" (Deuteronomy 11:11). That "waters" are truths—whether spiritual, rational, or scientific <note>original: *scientifica*, referring to knowledge based on the senses and memory</note>—is clear from these passages:

In Isaiah: "Behold, the Lord Jehovah Sabaoth <note>original: *Zebaoth*, meaning 'of Hosts'</note> is removing from Jerusalem and from Judah every staff of bread and every staff of water" (Isaiah 3:1).

In the same author: "He who walks in righteousness and speaks uprightly will dwell on high; his bread will be given, his waters will be faithful" (Isaiah 33:15–16). 

In the same author: "Then they will not thirst; He will lead them through the desert; He will make waters flow from the rock for them; and He splits the rock, and the waters flow out" (Isaiah 48:21; Exodus 17:1–8; Numbers 20:13). 

In David: "He split the rocks in the desert and gave them drink like the great depths; He brought streams out of the rock and made waters descend like a river" (Psalm 78:15–16). In this context, the "rock" stands for the Lord, and the "waters," "rivers," and "depths" coming from it stand for the truths that come from Him. 

In the same author: "Jehovah turns rivers into a desert and the outlets of waters into dry ground; He turns the desert into a pool of water and the thirsty land into outlets of waters" (Psalm 107:33, 35). 

In the same author: "The voice of Jehovah is upon the waters; Jehovah is upon many waters" (Psalm 29:3). 

In the same author: "There is a river whose streams will gladden the city of God, the holy place of the dwellings of the Most High" (Psalm 46:4 <note>Latin text cites verse 5</note>). 

In the same author: "By the word of Jehovah the heavens were made, and by the breath of His mouth all their host; gathering the waters of the sea like a heap, putting the depths into storehouses" (Psalm 33:6–7). 

In the same author: "You visit the earth and delight in it greatly, enriching it; the river of God is full of water" (Psalm 65:9 <note>Latin text cites verse 10</note>). 

In the same author: "The waters saw You, O God; the waters saw You and the depths were moved; the clouds poured out waters; Your way is in the sea, and Your path in many waters" (Psalm 77:16, 17, 19 <note>Latin text cites Psalm 67:17, 18, 20</note>). 

In this last passage, it is obvious to anyone that "waters" do not literally mean waters, nor were the "depths" physically moved, nor is Jehovah’s "way" literally in the sea or His "path" in waters. Rather, these terms signify spiritual things—that is, the spiritual things belonging to truth. Otherwise, this would simply be a heap of empty words.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of water as a spiritual symbol for truth, specifically examining how it was represented in Jewish rituals and its meaning in the context of Christian baptism and spiritual growth.</meta>

<header>G E N E S I S.</header>

"...twelve fruits," <note>original: *fructus duodecim*</note> Revelation 22:1–2. Because water signifies truths in the internal sense of the Word, several commands were given in the Jewish Church for the sake of representation before the angels (who view these rituals spiritually). It was commanded that the Priests and Levites wash themselves with water when they approached to minister, specifically from the Basin <note>original: *Labro*; the bronze laver used for ritual washing</note> between the Tent and the Altar, and later from the "Bronze Sea" and other basins around the Temple, which served as a fountain. 

Similarly, for the sake of representation, regulations were established concerning the *Water of Sin* (or purification) which was to be sprinkled on the Levites (Numbers 8:7). Also, regarding the *Water of Separation* made from the ashes of a red heifer (Numbers 19:2–19). Furthermore, the spoils taken from the Midianites were to be purified by water (Numbers 31:19–25). 

The *waters given from the Rock* (Exodus 17:1–8; Numbers 20:1–13; 23:13) represented and signified an abundance of spiritual things, or the truths of faith, from the Lord. The *bitter waters that were healed by wood* (Exodus 15:22–25) represented and signified truths that are not initially pleasing, but which become acceptable and pleasant through "good" or its affection. (That "Wood" signifies the "good" belonging to affection or the will, see number 643). 

From these examples, we can now understand what "Water" means in the Word, and consequently, what the "Water" in Baptism means. Regarding this, the Lord says in John: "Unless a man is born of Water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God" (John 3:5). In this context, Water is the spiritual side of faith, and the Spirit is its heavenly <note>original: *coeleste*; celestial</note> side. Thus, Baptism is a symbol of a person’s regeneration by the Lord through the truths and goods of faith. Regeneration does not happen *through* the act of Baptism itself, but through the life signified by Baptism—a life into which Christians enter because they possess the Word, which contains the truths of faith.

**2703.** **And she filled the skin with water:** This signifies truths from that source. This is evident from the significance of water as truth, as discussed above.

**2704.** **And she gave the boy a drink:** This signifies instruction in spiritual matters. This is clear from the significance of "giving a drink" <note>original: *potare*</note> as instructing in truths, and from the significance of "the boy" as the spiritual person in terms of truth (see number 2697). 

This state of instruction, described in this verse, is the *third state* of those who emerge from a process of "wastation" or desolation <note>original: *vastatione*; a process of being emptied of old ideas to make room for new truths</note>. When they reach the state of enlightenment or heavenly light (mentioned in verse 18; see number 2699), they are filled with an affection for knowing and learning truths. When they are in that affection, they are imbued with truths easily and almost naturally—those on earth from the Lord's Word or from Doctrine, and those in heaven from the Angels. The angels perceive nothing as more blessed or happy than teaching new arrivals (their "newly born brothers") and imbuing them with the truths and goods that belong to the heavenly Order and lead to the Lord.

<meta>This page continues the exposition of Genesis Chapter 21, specifically interpreting the spiritual meaning of the Lord's presence and the distinction between the "Spiritual" and "Celestial" heavens.</meta>

<page-num>45</page-num>

# CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE

That **God was with someone** <note>original: *esse Deus cum aliquo*</note> signifies the presence of the Lord, which can be understood without further explanation. The Lord is indeed present with everyone, for life comes from no other source; He governs the most minute details of everyone’s life, even among the worst people and in hell itself. However, He is present in different ways depending on how that life is received. In those who receive the life of His love for what is good and true but pervert it into a love for what is evil and false, the Lord is present and governs their intentions toward good as much as possible; yet, his presence with them is called "absence." This absence is measured by the degree to which evil is distant from good, and the false from the true. 

On the other hand, for those who receive the life of the Lord's love for what is good and true, "presence" is affirmed, specifically according to the degree of their reception. This can be compared to the sun, which is present through its heat and light in the plants of the world, also according to how they receive it. 

It was stated above that the **boy** <note>original: *puer*; referring here to Ishmael, who represents the spiritual man</note> signifies the spiritual aspect of truth. Here, it signifies "Spiritual People," because the boy represents the person of the Spiritual Church, the Spiritual Church itself, and—in a universal sense—the Lord's Spiritual Kingdom. When it is said that something signifies "the spiritual" (as this boy signifies the spiritual in relation to truth), it implies that it signifies spiritual people, for "the spiritual" does not exist without a subject. The same applies to other terms used in an abstract sense.

**2707. And he grew:** This signifies spiritual increases, which is evident without further explanation.

**2708. And he lived in the desert:** This signifies a state that is obscure by comparison. This is clear from the meaning of **to live** (which means to live spiritually, see number 2451) and from the meaning of a **desert** (which signifies a place with little vitality, see number 1927). Here, "the desert" means "obscure," but only by comparison. 

By "obscure by comparison" <note>original: *obscurum respective*</note> is meant the state of the **Spiritual Church** compared to the state of the **Celestial Church**, or the state of spiritual people compared to celestial people. 
* **Celestial people** are in the affection for what is good; **Spiritual people** are in the affection for what is true. 
* Celestials have **perception** <note>an immediate, intuitive knowledge of truth from the Lord</note>; Spirituals have the **dictate of conscience**. 
* To the Celestials, the Lord appears as a Sun; to the Spirituals, He appears as a Moon (see numbers 1521, 1530, 1531, 2495). 

To the Celestials, light is like a visual perception of good and truth from the Lord, similar to the light of day from the sun. But to the Spirituals, light from the Lord is like the light of night from the moon; thus, their state is obscure by comparison. The reason is that Celestials are in love with the Lord, and thus in the very life of the Lord; whereas Spirituals are in charity toward their neighbor and in faith, and while they are indeed in the life of the Lord, they are in it more obscurely. 

For this reason, Celestials never reason about faith and its truths; because they are in the perception of truth from good, they simply say, "It is so." Spirituals, however, speak and reason about the truths of faith because they are in a conscience of what is good derived from truth. Furthermore, for the Celestials, the "good of love" is implanted in the **will** <note>original: *parte voluntaria*</note>, where the primary life of man resides; but for the Spirituals, it is implanted in the **intellectual part** <note>original: *parte intellectuali*</note>, where the secondary life of man resides. This is why the Spirituals are in a state that is obscure by comparison (see numbers 81, 202, 337, 765, 784, 895, 1114 to 1125, 1155, 1577, 1824, 2048, 2088, 2227, 2454, 2507). This "relative obscurity" is what is called a **desert** here. 

In the Word, a **desert** <note>original: *Desertum*</note> signifies both what is sparsely inhabited and cultivated, and what is entirely uninhabited and uncultivated—it has a dual meaning. Where it signifies a place that is sparsely inhabited (where there are few dwellings, sheepfolds, pastures, and waters), it signifies that thing or those people who have relatively little life and light.

<meta>catchword: by comparison <note>original: *respective*</note></meta>

From these passages, it is clear what is signified by the words concerning **John the Baptist**: "This is he who was spoken of by Isaiah, saying: The voice of one crying in the *desert*, 'Prepare the way for the Lord, make His paths straight'" (**Matthew** <term>III: 3</term>; **Mark** <term>I: 3</term>; **Luke** <term>III: 4</term>; **John** <term>I: 23</term>; **Isaiah** <term>XL: 3</term>). Specifically, it means that at that time the Church was entirely devastated, so that there was no longer any good or any truth remaining. This is clearly shown by the fact that no one then knew that anything "internal" existed within a human being, nor that there was an internal meaning in the Word; thus, they did not know that the Messiah, or Christ, was coming to save them eternally. 

From this, it is also clear why John remained in the deserts until the day of his appearance to Israel (**Luke** <term>I: 80</term>), and why he preached in the *desert of Judea* (**Matthew** <term>III: 1</term>), and why he baptized in the desert (**Mark** <term>I: 4</term>). By doing so, he represented the actual state of the Church. 

Based on this meaning of the "desert," we can also understand why the Lord so often withdrew into the desert, as recorded in **Matthew** <term>IV: 1</term>; Chapter <term>XV: 32</term> to the end; **Mark** <term>I: 12, 13, 35</term> to <term>40, 45</term>; Chapter <term>VI: 31</term> to <term>36</term>; **Luke** <term>IV: 1</term>; Chapter <term>V: 16</term>; Chapter <term>IX: 10</term> and following; **John** <term>XI: 54</term>. Similarly, from the spiritual meaning of a "mountain," we can see why the Lord withdrew into the mountains, as in **Matthew** <term>IV: 23</term>; Chapter <term>XV: 29, 30, 31</term>; Chapter <term>XVII: 1</term> and following; Chapter <term>XXVIII: 16, 17</term>; **Mark** <term>III: 13, 14</term>; Chapter <term>VI: 46</term>; Chapter <term>IX: 2</term> to <term>9</term>; **Luke** <term>VI: 12, 13</term>; Chapter <term>IX: 28</term>; **John** <term>VI: 15</term>.

***

2709. **And he became a shooter of a bow.** That this signifies the man of the Spiritual Church is evident from the meaning of a "shot," a "missile," or an "arrow," which signifies truth; and from the meaning of a "bow," which signifies **doctrine** <note>the set of teachings or beliefs held by the church</note>, as discussed above in section 2686. 

The man of the Spiritual Church was called a "shooter of a bow" in ancient times because he defends himself by means of truths and debates about truths. This is different from the man of the Celestial Church, who is safe because of his focus on "good" and does not debate about truths (see section 2708). The truths by which the spiritual man defends himself and debates are derived from the Doctrine which he acknowledges. 

That the spiritual man was formerly called a "shooter" and "archer," and that Doctrine was called a "bow" and "quiver," and the truths of doctrine (or rather, its teachings) were called "missiles," "darts," and "arrows," is further established in **David**:

> "The children of Ephraim, being armed and *shooters of the bow*, turned back in the day of battle."

# CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE

In **Psalm 78:9**, Ephraim represents the intellectual aspect of the Church. In the **Book of Judges**: "You who ride on white donkeys, sitting on Middim <note>original: *Middim*; likely referring to judgments or luxurious carpets</note>, and walking on the way, meditate! Away from the noise of the archers <note>original: *Sagittariorum*</note> among the water-drawers, there they shall recount the righteous acts of Jehovah, the righteous acts of his villages in Israel" <term>V: 10, 11</term>. 

In **Isaiah**: "Jehovah called me from the womb; from the bowels of my mother he made mention of my name, and he made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hid me, and he made me a *polished arrow*; in his quiver he hid me, and said to me, 'You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified'" <term>XLIX: 1, 2, 3</term>. Here, Israel represents the **Spiritual Church**. 

In **David** <note>The Book of Psalms</note>: "Like *arrows* in the hand of a mighty man, so are the children of one's youth; blessed is everyone who has filled *his quiver with them*" <term>Psalm CXXVII: 4</term>. Here, the quiver represents the doctrine of good and truth. 

In **Habakkuk**: "The sun and moon stood in their habitation; at the light of *your arrows* they shall go, at the brightness of the lightning of your spear" <term>III: 11</term>. 

The account where Joash, King of Israel, at the command of Elisha, shot an *arrow from a bow* through a window—at which point Elisha said, "The *arrow of Jehovah’s salvation, the arrow of Jehovah’s salvation* against Syria" <note>original citation 2 Sam 13:16-18; the event actually occurs in 2 Kings 13:16-18</note>—signifies the secrets <term>arcana</term> concerning the Doctrine of good and truth. 

Just as most things in the Word also have an opposite sense, so do darts, weapons, arrows, the bow, and the archer; in that sense, they signify falsities, the doctrine of falsity, and those who are in falsity. For example, in **Moses**: "Joseph is a fruitful son, a fruitful son by a spring; his daughters walk upon the wall; they have treated him with bitterness, and *shot at him*, and the *archers* <note>original: *Sagittarii*</note> hated him" <term>Genesis XLIX: 22, 23</term>.

In **David**: "They sharpen their tongue like a sword; they aim *their arrow*, even bitter words, to *shoot* in secret at the upright; suddenly they *shoot* and do not fear him; they strengthen themselves in an evil word; they talk of hiding snares" <term>Psalm LXIV: 4, 5, 6</term>. 

In the same author: "Behold, the wicked bend the *bow*; they prepare *their arrow* on the string, to shoot in the darkness at those who are upright in heart" <term>Psalm XI: 2</term>. 

And again: "His truth is a shield and buckler; you shall not be afraid of the terror of the night, nor of the *arrow* that flies by day" <term>Psalm XCI: 5</term>.

**2710.** In this verse, the state of the Spiritual Church is described: specifically, that it is obscure compared to the state of the Celestial Church <note>The "Celestial Church" acts from love and perception, while the "Spiritual Church" acts from faith and intellect</note>, and that it is a state of conflict. This is because a person of the Spiritual Church does not know truth from any other source than doctrine, rather than from "good" itself, as the celestial person does.

**2711.** *Verse 21. And he lived in the desert of Paran; and his mother took a wife for him from the land of Egypt.* 
**"He lived in the desert of Paran"** signifies the life of the spiritual man regarding "good." **"The desert"** here, as before, signifies a relative obscurity. **"Paran"** signifies illumination from the Lord's Divine Human. **"And his mother took [him a wife]"** signifies the affection for truth. **"A wife from the land of Egypt"** signifies the affection for scientific knowledge <note>original: *scientiarum*; the factual or external knowledge</note> which belongs to the man of the Spiritual Church.

**2712.** **"He lived in the desert of Paran"**: That this signifies the life of the spiritual man regarding good is clear from the meaning of "to live" (or "to dwell"), which is a term applied to the concept of "good."

# GENESIS

...regarding the good of truth, or spiritual good—that is, the good of the spiritual person. The nature of this good is described by the statement that he "dwelt in the wilderness of Paran," which follows shortly. The fact that "dwelling" <note>original: *habitare*</note> is used to describe the good or the affection for truth is clear from many places in the Word <note>The Bible</note> where "cities" are discussed. In these passages, cities signify truths, and it is said they will be without an "inhabitant" <note>original: *habitator*</note>, which signifies good (see numbers 2268, 2450, 2451). This is because truths are "inhabited" by good; truths without good are like a city where no one lives. 

We see this in **Zephaniah**: "I have made their streets waste, so that no one passes by; their cities are desolate, so that there is **not a single inhabitant**" <term>III: 6</term>. 

In **Jeremiah**: "Jehovah, who led us through the wilderness... where no man passes through and no person has dwelt... they have made the land a wasteland; its cities are burned, so there is **no inhabitant**" <term>II: 6, 15</term>. 

In the same prophet: "Every city is forsaken, and **no one dwells in them**" <term>IV: 29</term>. 

And again: "In the desolate streets of Jerusalem, where there is no man, **no inhabitant**, and no beast" <term>XXXIII: 10</term>. In this context, "streets" represent truths (n: 2336), "no man" represents a lack of celestial good, "no inhabitant" represents a lack of spiritual good, and "no beast" represents a lack of natural good. 

In **Jeremiah**: "The cities of Moab shall be a desolation, with **no one dwelling in them**" <term>XLVIII: 9</term>. 

In the Prophets, every expression involves a "marriage" between truth and good. Therefore, when a city is called "desolate," the text also adds that there is "no inhabitant." This is because "city" signifies truths and "inhabitant" signifies good; otherwise, saying there is "no inhabitant" after saying the city is "desolate" would be redundant. 

Similarly, there are specific terms used to signify things belonging to celestial good, spiritual good, and truth. In **Isaiah**: "Your offspring shall **possess** the nations, and they shall **inhabit** the desolate cities" <term>LIV: 3</term>. Here, "possessing" describes celestial good, while "inhabiting" describes spiritual good. 

In the same prophet: "My chosen ones shall **possess** it, and my servants shall **dwell** there" <term>LXV: 9</term>, using the same distinction. 

In **David** <note>The Book of Psalms</note>: "God will save Zion and build the cities of Judah; and they shall **dwell** there and **possess** it. The offspring of His servants shall inherit it, and those who love His Name shall **dwell** in it" <term>Psalm LXIX: 36, 37</term>. Here, "dwelling and possessing together" describes celestial good, while "dwelling" on its own describes spiritual good. 

In **Isaiah**: "Saying to Jerusalem, 'You shall be **inhabited**,' and to the cities of Judah, 'You shall be built'" <term>XLIV: 26</term>. Here, "inhabiting" is used to describe the good of the Spiritual Church, which is represented by Jerusalem. 

In fact, words in the Word are so specifically applied to their respective types of good and truth that one can know the general subject matter simply by recognizing these specific terms.

**2713.** A **wilderness** <note>original: *desertum*</note> signifies a state of relative obscurity. This is because a wilderness represents obscurity when applied to a "spiritual" person in comparison to a "celestial" person (as discussed above in number 2708).

**2714.** **Paran** signifies enlightenment from the Lord’s **Divine Human** <note>The Lord's glorified humanity</note>. This is evident from the places in the Word where Paran is mentioned, such as in the prophet **Habakkuk**: "Jehovah, I have heard your fame and was afraid; O Jehovah, revive your work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make it known; in your wrath remember mercy. God will come from Teman, and the Holy One from **Mount Paran**, Selah; His glory covered the heavens..." <term>III: 2, 3</term>.

In these trials, man often fails, but the Lord wins the victory on his behalf. Consequently, these journeys also represent the Lord's own temptations and victories. Because the Lord endured these temptations through His **Divine Human**, the "wilderness of Paran" here likewise signifies the Lord's **Divine Human**. 

The same meaning is found in these words from the same author:
